scenario_en: You manage marketing for a basement waterproofing company. Lately the work coming out of your two coordinators is sloppy: typos on postcards, late social posts, missed deadlines. Truth is, you've been skipping your own proofing step and turning in your budget report late every month. The owner asks what's going on with your department.
option_a_en: Add a triple sign-off rule so nothing goes out without three approvals.
option_b_en: Replace your weakest coordinator — somebody has to set the tone.
option_c_en: Fix your own habits first. Proof your work, hit your deadlines, and let the team see it.
why_en: A department reflects its leader. The team is copying what you model, not what you say. New rules and new people won't fix a standard the leader isn't living.
principle_voice_en: Your business is your elongated shadow.

scenario_en: Spring leads came in 30% under goal. A Google algorithm update hurt rankings, and it rained out one home show. But you also mailed the postcards three weeks late and never tested the new landing page. Tomorrow you present results to the owner, and it would be easy to lead with the weather and Google.
option_a_en: Own it. List what you did and didn't do, then present your fix plan.
option_b_en: Report that the Google update caused the miss — it's technically true.
option_c_en: Ask for a bigger budget to make up the gap.
why_en: The marketplace gave you what you deserved. Blaming circumstances guarantees a repeat; owning the late mail and untested page is the only path to different results next spring.
principle_voice_en: The world and the marketplace is giving you exactly what you deserve right now.

scenario_en: Your big home show booth flopped: 9 leads against a goal of 60. You spent $8,000, staffed it all weekend, and watched competitors' booths stay busy. Monday morning you're embarrassed and the owner wants a recap. Part of you wants to declare home shows dead.
option_a_en: Recommend the company swear off home shows — the channel clearly doesn't work.
option_b_en: Run a full debrief — booth location, signage, staffing, scripts — and rebuild the show system before the next one.
option_c_en: Tell the owner the promoter's foot traffic was weak this year.
why_en: A setback is poison or fuel — you choose. Competitors' busy booths prove the channel works; your system failed. Turning the flop into a corrected system is how the pain pays you back.
principle_voice_en: The story you tell yourself about your past should be fuel, not poison.

scenario_en: You've run marketing the same way for three years. A respected industry course on internet marketing is open now, but it's busy season and you'd have to give up two evenings a week for six weeks. Your cost per lead has been creeping up and you're not sure why.
option_a_en: Enroll now and block weekly learning time on your calendar — treat it like an appointment.
option_b_en: Wait until winter when things slow down.
option_c_en: Skip it — you learn plenty on the job.
why_en: Work harder on yourself than on your job. Rising cost per lead is a knowledge problem; "too busy to learn" keeps you exactly where you are. Slow season never really comes.
principle_voice_en: Once we think we know it all, we stop learning.

scenario_en: You have $5,000 of flex budget. A trendy short-video campaign is tempting and the owner's son keeps pushing it. Meanwhile, the basics are leaking: crews place yard signs on maybe half the jobs, web leads sit overnight, and a third of leads never get entered in the CRM with a source.
option_a_en: Launch the video campaign — you have to be where the attention is.
option_b_en: Do both halfway: a small video test and a memo about the basics.
option_c_en: Fix the basics first — sign on every job, every lead in the CRM, fast callbacks — then experiment.
why_en: Simple things done without fail beat clever things done sometimes. New traffic poured into a leaky system is wasted money; the basics are free and compounding.
principle_voice_en: Simple things are easy to do, and easy not to do.

scenario_en: The owner storms in: "Leads are down — what's happening?" You have hunches: maybe the radio spots faded, maybe a competitor's new truck wraps are stealing attention. But your tracking is patchy and you honestly don't know which channel slipped. He wants an answer right now.
option_a_en: Share your gut read confidently — leaders should sound decisive.
option_b_en: Say "Give me 48 hours," then pull real numbers by channel before recommending anything.
option_c_en: Promise a new campaign on the spot so you look like you're acting.
why_en: To set things right you have to see things right. Acting on hunches treats the wrong channel and burns budget. Honest "I'll find out" beats confident guessing every time.
principle_voice_en: To set things right, you must see things right.

scenario_en: The owner approves $30,000 for a spring direct-mail drop — your biggest ever. The printer is pushing you to get files in this week to hit his press schedule. You haven't set a lead goal, picked test lists, computed allowable cost per lead, or planned how the call center will handle response.
option_a_en: Mail now to the biggest list you can afford and adjust as results come in.
option_b_en: Build the model first — goal, allowable cost per lead, test cells, response plan — then print.
option_c_en: Let the printer design the piece and choose the list; he does this all day.
why_en: Everything is created twice — first on paper, then in the world. Modeling flushes out problems while they're still free to fix. A printer's deadline is not a plan.
principle_voice_en: If you don't plan your future, it's a pretty good indication you aren't interested in it.

scenario_en: Your yard sign program requires crews to place a sign at every job and text a photo. Compliance is at 40% and crews roll their eyes — "we're installers, not marketers." You could tighten enforcement, or you could explain something you've never actually told them.
option_a_en: Show them the why: a $3.50 sign creates a $200 lead from a trusting neighbor — then re-train the how.
option_b_en: Add a penalty for every missing photo.
option_c_en: Drop the program — you can't force people to care.
why_en: If there is no why, the how doesn't matter. People who understand that one sign can pay for weeks of signs will place them; punished people will game photos and resent you.
principle_voice_en: People will not come to work each day fired up to give their best to make you money. There must be something more.

scenario_en: You've personally staffed every home show booth for two years — nights, weekends, holidays. Your spouse is fed up and you're burning out, but you tell yourself nobody captures leads like you do. Three shows are coming up in six weeks, including one on your anniversary.
option_a_en: Keep working every show yourself — that's dedication.
option_b_en: Ask the owner to drop home shows; they cost you too many weekends.
option_c_en: Build and train a show team with a rotation, scripts, and a per-appointment incentive — then take your anniversary off.
why_en: The business should give you more of a life, not less. A function that only works when you sacrifice your life isn't a system — it's a trap you built for yourself.
principle_voice_en: Freedom comes when you realize you can't do it alone.

principle_title_en: Do Right When It Costs You
scenario_en: Your 20,000-piece postcard went out with a typo: "$500 off" instead of "$50 off." Calls are coming in. Honoring it could cost the company $40,000 if everyone redeems. The call center manager asks what to tell people. The owner is traveling and unreachable until tonight.
option_a_en: Honor it quietly — but only for callers who push back when corrected.
option_b_en: Honor the printed offer for everyone who calls, and own the mistake to the owner tonight.
option_c_en: Tell the call center to say it was a misprint and quote the real discount.
why_en: Your word in print is your word. Most callers won't redeem, but every caller will remember how you handled it. "Misprint" is the convenient choice that trades reputation for dollars.
principle_voice_en: We don't need upset people out there with Internet connections.

principle_title_en: Hiring Makes You or Breaks You
scenario_en: Your marketing coordinator quit and the busy season starts in six weeks. After two weeks of searching you have one candidate: she's okay — decent resume, flat interview, no spark. The work is piling up on your desk and the owner says "just get somebody in the seat."
option_a_en: Keep recruiting hard — widen the posting, work your network, restart the search if needed.
option_b_en: Hire the okay candidate; a warm body beats an empty desk in busy season.
option_c_en: Skip the hire and quietly absorb the work yourself.
why_en: People choices decide nearly everything. A mediocre hire costs months of management, redone work, and a second search anyway. Short-term pain beats a year of managing a mistake.
principle_voice_en: Hiring will make you, or break you. Too often contractors spend 1% of their time recruiting and 99% of their time managing their recruiting mistakes.

scenario_en: Two finalists for your digital marketing seat. One has a stunning portfolio and certifications — but trashed her last employer in the interview, and her dates didn't match her resume. The other is greener with modest samples, but honest, hungry, and her references rave about her attitude.
option_a_en: Hire the portfolio — skills pay the bills; you'll just watch her closely.
option_b_en: Hire neither and repost the job at a higher salary.
option_c_en: Hire the character. You can teach ad platforms; you can't teach honesty.
why_en: Skills are trainable; character isn't. Someone who badmouths an employer and bends a resume will eventually do both to you — with your ad budget and your brand in her hands.
principle_voice_en: We don't get people to adopt our core values. We find people who already have them.

scenario_en: After a long search, your final candidate for events coordinator is... pretty good. Checks the boxes, pleasant enough, nothing wrong on paper. Your team is split. You keep telling yourself you should be excited, but you're not. The search has already taken nine weeks and you're tired.
option_a_en: Hire — pretty good beats an empty desk, and the search is exhausting.
option_b_en: Offer a vague 90-day "tryout" to hedge your doubts.
option_c_en: Don't hire. If it's not "Hell yeah," it's no — restart the search.
why_en: Lukewarm at hiring becomes lukewarm at work. Your hesitation is data. Sometimes the best hiring decision is the one you don't make — a tryout just postpones the same no.
principle_voice_en: If you don't love the candidate, don't hire.

scenario_en: Your coordinator Dana lights up a home show booth — visitors love her, appointments stack up. But she also owns your lead-tracking spreadsheet, and it's a disaster: wrong sources, missing entries, formulas broken. You've corrected her three times. She dreads the spreadsheet and says so.
option_a_en: Put her on a performance plan for the tracking work.
option_b_en: Move Dana to own events and shows full-time; put a detail-loving person on tracking.
option_c_en: Let her go — accuracy matters in marketing.
why_en: Match strengths to where they're needed and weaknesses to where they don't matter. Dana isn't a bad employee — she's a great events person stuck in a numbers seat.
principle_voice_en: Everybody is right for some job.

scenario_en: Your new lead-intake coordinator keeps making CRM mistakes — wrong sources, duplicate records, leads marked dead that aren't. You realize you never actually trained her; she just shadowed the last coordinator for two days before that person left. You're slammed with the spring campaign and training would take real hours.
option_a_en: Build a real training plan — written process, side-by-side reps, checkpoints — and train her properly.
option_b_en: Fire her and hire someone who "gets it."
option_c_en: Let her keep figuring it out by shadowing old notes — you're too busy right now.
why_en: You can't hold someone accountable to training they never got. "Too busy to train" means paying for her mistakes forever — what if you don't train her and she stays?
principle_voice_en: Shadowing alone yields a copy of a copy of a copy.

scenario_en: You still personally write every Facebook post, design every flyer, and lay out every postcard — because you're good at it and it's fun. Meanwhile the annual plan is half-done, the agency goes unmanaged, and nobody has reviewed channel numbers in a month. Your coordinator has asked twice to take on the creative work.
option_a_en: Work nights so you can do both the creative and the leading.
option_b_en: Skip the planning — posts and flyers are what actually generate leads.
option_c_en: Train your coordinator to own the creative; you set standards, review, and lead the function.
why_en: You're paid for the team's results, not your handiwork. Every hour you spend designing flyers is an hour the whole department goes unled — and your willing coordinator goes undeveloped.
principle_voice_en: If you're doing a job in your business, you're in the way.

scenario_en: You're hiring an agency to run Google Ads — $4,000 a month. They're polished and say "just give us access and relax; we'll handle everything." You're tempted: one less thing on your plate, and they're the experts. The contract is on your desk.
option_a_en: Hand over the login and check back next quarter — that's why you hired experts.
option_b_en: Set cost-per-lead targets, require weekly reporting, schedule monthly reviews — then let them work.
option_c_en: Don't sign; keep running the ads yourself at night.
why_en: Delegation means clear goals, measures, and reporting — abdication means handing off and hoping. If an unmanaged agency burns your budget, the fault is yours, not theirs.
principle_voice_en: Deputize, don't surrender ownership.

scenario_en: Your new Showtimer let weekend home-show leads sit for four days before calling. You're furious — stale show leads barely set. Then you check yourself: you handed her the lead box and said "work these," but never told her the standard was every lead called within 24 hours.
option_a_en: Set the expectation first — written 24-hour standard, why it matters — then hold her to it.
option_b_en: Write her up; common sense says you call leads fast.
option_c_en: Quietly take the show leads back and call them yourself.
why_en: Expectation gaps cause execution gaps. She failed a standard that existed only in your head. Set it clearly once, and you've earned the right to enforce it forever.
principle_voice_en: If you don't tell your team what you expect, they can't be accountable to it.

scenario_en: Your coordinator just delivered the best lead month in company history — she rebuilt the review-request system on her own initiative and Google reviews doubled. You have a small discretionary budget. She's quiet and never asks for attention, so it would be easy to just nod and move on.
option_a_en: Announce it at the company meeting, hand her a handwritten note, and add a surprise gift.
option_b_en: Quietly add $50 to her paycheck — money talks.
option_c_en: Say nothing; doing great work is what she's paid for.
why_en: Recognition beats money. Fifty silent dollars vanishes into a paycheck; public praise and a handwritten note get kept for years — and tell the whole team what gets celebrated here.
principle_voice_en: Handwritten notes end up on walls for years.

principle_title_en: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool
scenario_en: Your dependable coordinator has been distracted for two weeks — missed deadlines, short answers, a postcard error that cost $600. Today you learn from a teammate that her mother was just diagnosed with cancer. The spring campaign deadline is in ten days and you need her at full speed.
option_a_en: Start documenting the misses for her personnel file, just in case.
option_b_en: Stay out of her personal life; results are results.
option_c_en: Sit down with her, ask how you can help, flex her schedule, and cover the gaps yourself.
why_en: People run through walls for leaders who genuinely care about them as humans. Compassion now buys loyalty for years; cold documentation now loses her the moment things stabilize.
principle_voice_en: Every time you talk to someone, you leave them bigger or smaller; the choice is yours.

principle_title_en: Give Away the Credit, Take the Blame
scenario_en: Your team's review-generation push tripled Google reviews this quarter — the owner is thrilled and praises you in the leadership meeting. Same meeting: the botched radio buy you approved gets raised, and your coordinator who placed the order is sitting right there. All eyes turn to you for both items.
option_a_en: Accept the praise graciously and note the radio buy "had several hands on it."
option_b_en: Name your team for the review win; take the radio mistake yourself — you approved it.
option_c_en: Stay neutral on both — credit and blame games are politics.
why_en: Leaders pass credit down and pull blame up. Your coordinator executing your approved buy is your mistake. Teams give everything for leaders who shield them and spotlight them.
principle_voice_en: In a rally speech, the leader gives away all the credit, and takes all the blame.

principle_title_en: Never Act on One Side of a Story
scenario_en: A top salesperson corners you: "Your new lead coordinator is sending me junk leads and holding back the good ones for her favorites. Fix it or I'm going to the owner." He's your biggest producer and he's angry. The coordinator is at lunch. Your finger is on the reassign button.
option_a_en: Hold off. Hear the coordinator's side and pull the lead-distribution records before changing anything.
option_b_en: Reassign lead routing today to calm your top producer, then sort it out later.
option_c_en: Tell the salesperson to take it up with the coordinator directly.
why_en: One side of a story is half a story. The records may show even distribution — or a real problem. Acting on the loudest voice teaches everyone that anger beats facts.
principle_voice_en: Never argue with — or undercut — your people based on one account; nothing should escape your attention.

scenario_en: A two-star Google review just posted: "Nice work, but they tracked mud everywhere and never called back." It's one review among ninety good ones, and responding means an awkward call. The crew involved says the customer is exaggerating. It would be easy to let it scroll down the page.
option_a_en: Reply publicly with a defense of the crew's side.
option_b_en: Call the customer today, listen, fix it, then respond publicly showing you made it right.
option_c_en: Ignore it — one bad review out of ninety is statistical noise.
why_en: Small problems handled today stay small. An ignored reviewer escalates and a defensive reply shows every future prospect how you treat complaints. Speed turns a critic into a referral.
principle_voice_en: If you don't do things right when you are small, you will never get the opportunity to be big.

principle_title_en: Culture Is When the Boss Leaves
scenario_en: You're out for a week at a conference. Returning, you learn your team skipped the daily lead-review huddle all five days, and weekend web leads waited until Monday. Nothing "broke" — but everything you thought was culture turned out to be supervision. The team seems sheepish but unworried.
option_a_en: Cancel future conferences; clearly you can't leave.
option_b_en: Install software that logs response times so you can monitor remotely.
option_c_en: Rebuild it as their standard: explain the why, name an owner for the huddle, and let the team run it.
why_en: Culture is what happens when the boss leaves. If standards live only in your presence, you built compliance, not culture. Ownership and understood purpose survive your absence; surveillance doesn't.
principle_voice_en: One rally speech is not culture — repeat it everywhere, constantly.

scenario_en: In your campaign-planning meeting, a junior coordinator says, "Honestly, I think the new radio spots sound cheesy — my neighbors laughed at one." You wrote those spots. The room goes quiet, watching how you'll react. You feel your face flush.
option_a_en: Thank her, ask her to say more, and suggest testing both versions with real prospects.
option_b_en: Defend the creative — explain why the spots work and move the agenda along.
option_c_en: Smile, say "noted," and never bring it up again.
why_en: Shoot the messenger once and you'll never get truth again. Her neighbors are your market — that's free research. The prospect's opinion rules, not the author's pride.
principle_voice_en: It doesn't matter what you think; it matters what prospects think.

scenario_en: Your postcard promotion is generating calls, but the call center is drowning — hold times are long and the manager says callers are hanging up. Strictly speaking, that's her department's problem; your job was generating the response, and your next campaign is due. She hasn't formally asked for help.
option_a_en: Note it in your report so leadership knows the call center is the bottleneck.
option_b_en: Walk over today — share the response forecast, stagger your next drop, lend a trained body for peak hours.
option_c_en: Pause all marketing until the call center staffs up.
why_en: There is one department: customer service. Leads you generate and then watch die on hold are your dead leads. Internal handoffs are yours to follow to completion, not to document.
principle_voice_en: No matter where you work, there is one department — the customer service department.

principle_title_en: Serve the Human, Not the House
scenario_en: You're writing the company's new website copy. The draft is full of specs: pump models, drainage capacity, warranty terms. Reading customer reviews for quotes, you notice nobody mentions equipment — they write about sleeping through rainstorms, saving grandma's photo albums, kids playing in a dry basement.
option_a_en: Keep the spec-driven copy; serious buyers want technical proof.
option_b_en: Split the difference — specs up top, a testimonial section below.
option_c_en: Rewrite around the homeowner's life — peace of mind, protected memories — with specs as support.
why_en: You're not servicing a house; you're servicing a human being who owns the home. Customers buy relief and safety, not pump models. Your reviews just handed you the message.
principle_voice_en: We are not servicing a house, we are servicing a human being who owns the home.

scenario_en: Referral leads close at twice the rate of paid leads and cost almost nothing, but referrals are flat. The production manager mentions crews finish jobs fine — clean enough, polite enough — but nothing memorable happens at the end. You have budget you could spend on more paid ads instead.
option_a_en: Build a Wow finish with production — final walkthrough, small surprise gift, leave it cleaner — then make referring easy.
option_b_en: Buy more paid leads; referrals can't be manufactured.
option_c_en: Mail past customers $100 referral bounty cards and call it done.
why_en: Satisfied customers tell no one — thrilled customers refer. Wow creates the reciprocity that drives the cheapest, best leads there are. A bounty without a Wow pays people to recommend "fine."
principle_voice_en: Merely satisfied customers call it a fair transaction and tell no one.

principle_title_en: The Experience Is Half the Product
scenario_en: A mystery-shop of your own company rattles you: phone answered on the sixth ring, the web form's auto-reply reads like a robot, and the confirmation email has a broken logo. The actual installation work is excellent. Your planned project this month was a billboard campaign.
option_a_en: Run the billboard — awareness is marketing's job; phone manners belong to operations.
option_b_en: Fix the touchpoints first — two-ring standard, warm scripts, rewritten emails — then buy media.
option_c_en: Add "great customer service" as a tagline on the billboard.
why_en: Every touchpoint is a Moment of Truth where customers judge the whole company. Great installation can't outweigh a shabby first impression — and billboards just send more people into the bad experience.
principle_voice_en: Customers judge your professionalism at the fragile moment of deciding whom to invite into their home.

scenario_en: Your email blast went out with the wrong sale dates — hundreds of customers now expect a discount weekend that doesn't exist. You caught it twenty minutes after sending. You could send a correction now and honor the dates, or wait and see how many people actually notice.
option_a_en: Send a same-hour correction owning the goof, and honor the printed dates anyway.
option_b_en: Wait a few days; if complaints stay quiet, no correction needed.
option_c_en: Honor the dates only for customers who call to ask.
why_en: Customers see your mistake as a test, and speed is the apology. Handled fast and generously, a goof can build more trust than a clean send. Waiting is the convenient choice that gambles your reputation.
principle_voice_en: Embedded in every problem is the opportunity to get better.

scenario_en: You have $6,000 left in the budget. Option one: a new-mover mailing list of strangers at roughly $300 per lead generated. Option two: your database of 4,200 past customers who haven't heard from the company in three years — no annual contact program exists. The owner says "your call."
option_a_en: Split it 50/50 so you're not putting all eggs in one basket.
option_b_en: Buy the new-mover list — growth means new customers.
option_c_en: Fund the past-customer program — annual letters, service reminders, anniversary check-ins.
why_en: Past customers already know and trust you, won't shop you, and cost a fraction to re-engage. New strangers cost hundreds per lead. Gold sitting in your database beats dirt you haven't dug.
principle_voice_en: You have a choice – let them go or keep them forever.

scenario_en: You're writing the spring campaign and the agency proposes scare tactics: a countdown timer that resets nightly, "ONLY 3 SLOTS LEFT" that isn't true, and stock photos of collapsed foundations. They say fear converts. Your inspectors do find real damage in most homes they visit — you have actual photos and stories.
option_a_en: Run the agency's version; conversion rates pay the bills.
option_b_en: Use real urgency — actual local damage photos, true stories, the honest word "yet."
option_c_en: Drop urgency completely; just list services and a phone number.
why_en: Selling is helping people fix real problems. Truthful urgency — real damage, real consequences of waiting — serves homeowners. Fake scarcity is the convenient shortcut that converts today and corrodes trust forever.
principle_voice_en: Build urgency honestly — use the word 'yet' and relive real past damage, not manufactured pressure.

scenario_en: Reviewing yesterday's web leads, your coordinator has flagged four to skip: a mobile-home address, a "low income" zip code, a misspelled inquiry, and a tiny repair request. "Not worth a salesperson's afternoon," she says. Each lead cost the company about $180 to generate. She's trying to protect the sales team's time.
option_a_en: Every lead gets full effort and a set appointment — coach her on why pre-judging kills companies.
option_b_en: Compromise: route the flagged leads to the rookie salesperson.
option_c_en: Approve her filter; respecting the sales team's time builds goodwill.
why_en: Judging who will buy changes behavior and causes them not to buy. Small repairs become referrals; "bad" zip codes hold paid-off houses. Leads belong to the company, not to anyone's opinion.
principle_voice_en: Leads are treated like cash – they are precious and must be accounted for.

scenario_en: Your coordinator wants to add a "ballpark pricing" page to the website and let phone reps quote rough numbers — "people just want an idea, and other companies do it." Calls do sometimes end when reps refuse to give prices. The sales manager is firmly against quoting before inspection.
option_a_en: Add the pricing page; transparency is what modern buyers expect.
option_b_en: Hold the line — train reps on a respectful script that sells the free inspection, never a number.
option_c_en: Let reps quote a wide range, like "$3,000 to $30,000."
why_en: A number given before value is built is the only thing the prospect remembers — and every real quote loses to it. No two homes are alike; the inspection is where value is created.
principle_voice_en: Never quote or confirm a price before inspection and presentation.

scenario_en: Cleaning up the CRM, you find 312 unsold proposals from the last 18 months — homeowners who got quotes and never bought. Nobody has contacted any of them since. Your coordinator suggests archiving them: "They went with someone else or changed their minds. Fresh leads matter more."
option_a_en: Archive them; chasing cold quotes annoys people.
option_b_en: Send one mass "still interested?" email and close whoever doesn't reply.
option_c_en: Build a Hunter program — call every unsold proposal on a schedule, forever, until they buy or say stop.
why_en: Homeowners you don't close buy from someone within six months — or they're still waiting. Those 312 quotes are paid-for leads with known projects. Follow up forever; "no" today isn't "no" in March.
principle_voice_en: What will be different in 6 months?

scenario_en: Friday 4:55 pm. Three web leads just landed and your lead coordinator is packing up — "I'll call them Monday." You know each lead cost about $220 to generate, and weekend shoppers will call your competitors tomorrow morning. Monday is two and a half days away.
option_a_en: Stop her — those leads get called in the next ten minutes, and you fix weekend coverage permanently.
option_b_en: Let it ride; Monday morning calls are standard business hours.
option_c_en: Send the leads an automated email so they feel acknowledged until Monday.
why_en: Leads are cash, and cash left on the table over a weekend dies. A lead called in minutes converts at many times the rate of one called Monday. You paid $660 for those three names.
principle_voice_en: Leads are treated like cash – they are precious and must be accounted for.

scenario_en: Budget season. The owner asks which channels to cut and which to double. You run radio, postcards, Google Ads, two home shows, and yard signs — but call takers rarely ask "how did you hear about us?", and a third of CRM entries say source "unknown." Your gut says radio works.
option_a_en: Recommend from experience; you've watched these channels for years.
option_b_en: Fix attribution first — mandatory source question, tracking numbers per channel — and decide on real data next quarter.
option_c_en: Cut the most expensive channel; expensive is where waste hides.
why_en: Everything comes out to a number, and you can't take the right action on numbers you don't have. A wrong gut call could kill your best channel and fund your worst one.
principle_voice_en: Business is not a mystery. With controlled inputs, we can get predictable outputs. You're in the arithmetic business.

scenario_en: The owner tells you to cut the marketing budget 20 percent this quarter. Your instinct is to trim a little from every channel so nothing dies. Your media buyer warns that spreading the cut everywhere will starve your winners along with your losers.
option_a_en: Cut every channel by 20 percent evenly. It is fair and fast, and every vendor shares the pain. No single channel collapses, and you can restore funding next quarter.
option_b_en: Pause the two newest channels entirely and protect the proven ones at full funding. New experiments are the riskiest spend, and the owner asked for a cut.
option_c_en: Gather the team, show the real cost-per-lead by channel, and cut the losers completely while protecting the winners. Tell the owner plainly which cuts hurt.
why_en: It turns a cut into a performance decision driven by real numbers, and it protects the people producing results instead of punishing everyone equally.
principle_voice_en: Business is not a mystery. With controlled inputs, we can get predictable outputs. You're in the arithmetic business.

scenario_en: Maria, your star coordinator, is the only one who knows the home-show checklist, the review-request timing, and where the lead sources map in the CRM — it's all in her head. She just gave notice: she leaves in three weeks for a family move. The team is in mild panic.
option_a_en: Have her train one teammate verbally as the new go-to person.
option_b_en: Spend the three weeks documenting every process — written playbooks, checklists, recorded walkthroughs — then cross-train the team.
option_c_en: Offer her a big raise and remote work to stay.
why_en: A department that lives in one head isn't a system, it's a hostage situation. Documented playbooks survive any departure. Training one new hero just rebuilds the same fragile setup with a different name.
principle_voice_en: Simple plans, flawlessly executed, beat complicated plans never put into practice.

principle_title_en: How We Do Anything Is How We Do Everything
scenario_en: Friday afternoon. A batch of 200 yard signs arrives from the printer — the company red is noticeably off and your phone number prints small and fuzzy. Crews need signs Monday and reordering takes ten days. They're "just" $3.50 yard signs, and you're tempted to shrug and ship them out.
option_a_en: Use them — homeowners won't study a lawn sign's color accuracy.
option_b_en: Use this batch now but make the printer fix the next order.
option_c_en: Reject the batch, get a rush reprint, and bridge Monday with the older correct signs on hand.
why_en: How we do anything is how we do everything. A fuzzy number is a dead lead, and off-brand red erodes every other impression you've paid for. The $3.50 sign gets the same excellence as the $50,000 job.
principle_voice_en: How we do anything is how we do everything. We can't have exceptions to our standards and behavior.

scenario_en: You manage the Appointment Center. Lately you've been dragging in at 8:55, calling marketing's leads "junk" within earshot, and skipping the morning huddle. By noon today you hear your reps sighing at callers and tagging leads "junk" in the CRM. Energy on the floor is flat, and you catch yourself blaming the team.
option_a_en: Post a positivity policy and warn that bad attitudes will be written up.
option_b_en: Fix yourself first: arrive early, work the floor smiling, restart huddles, never trash a lead out loud again.
option_c_en: Pull your two grumpiest reps aside and coach them on phone tone.
why_en: The department is a mirror of its leader. The reps didn't invent the sighing — they copied it. Policies and coaching can't outrun the shadow you cast every morning.
principle_voice_en: Your business is your elongated shadow.

scenario_en: Your AC missed the monthly appointment goal by 14%. Real things went wrong: marketing's lead volume dipped, two reps were out sick, and the CRM crashed for half a day. The owner sits down and asks, "What happened?"
option_a_en: Own it: "I didn't flex shifts, push recycling, or call leads myself. Here's my fix plan."
option_b_en: Present an accurate, fair list of the outside causes — they really did happen.
option_c_en: Point out the sales team missed too, and ask the owner to push marketing for more leads.
why_en: The causes were real, but a leader who answers with causes stays at 86% forever. Total responsibility is the only answer that produces a different next month.
principle_voice_en: The world and the marketplace is giving you exactly what you deserve right now.

scenario_en: You're a rep. Yesterday you lost a huge commercial lead by quoting the wrong crew availability, and the salesperson chewed you out by the coffee machine in front of everyone. This morning your stomach knots when the phone board lights up.
option_a_en: Ask to work data entry for a few days until it blows over.
option_b_en: Remind yourself the lead sheet from marketing was sloppy anyway.
option_c_en: Write down exactly what went wrong, fix your availability sheet today, and take the next call sharper.
why_en: A setback becomes poison or fuel depending on the story you tell yourself. Hiding and blaming both burn the lesson; extracting the fix turns yesterday's pain into today's edge.
principle_voice_en: Embedded in every problem is the opportunity to get better.

scenario_en: The company starts optional Friday call-review sessions where reps listen to recordings of their own calls with the group. You're the veteran with the best set rate in the building. The session conflicts with your easiest paperwork hour.
option_a_en: Attend — and bring your worst call of the week to dissect in front of everyone.
option_b_en: Skip it; your numbers prove you don't need it. Let the strugglers go.
option_c_en: Attend, but play your best call so the new reps can learn from it.
why_en: The moment you think you know it all, you stop growing. The top performer studying their worst tape sets the learning culture for the whole room — and finds the next gear.
principle_voice_en: Once we think we know it all, we stop learning.

scenario_en: You're halfway through typing careful CRM notes from your last call when the phone hits ring two. Your only floor-mate is already on a call. Voicemail will catch it at ring four, and the caller can always leave a message.
option_a_en: Finish the notes — accuracy matters, and that's what voicemail is for.
option_b_en: Answer by ring two, smiling, and flag your notes to finish the moment you hang up.
option_c_en: Answer, then immediately ask the caller to hold while you finish typing.
why_en: Answer in two rings is the basic the whole machine rests on. A caller who hits voicemail calls the next company. The convenient choice quietly costs a paid-for lead.
principle_voice_en: Simple things are easy to do — and easy not to do.

scenario_en: Your set rate has slid three straight months: 96%, 91%, 87%. The team meeting starts in an hour. You're tempted to open with an upbeat pep talk so nobody panics, since morale already feels shaky.
option_a_en: Promise a pizza party if the team climbs back to 95%.
option_b_en: Tell the team "we're still better than most companies" — which is true.
option_c_en: Put the rep-by-rep, source-by-source numbers on the wall, name the slide out loud, then build the fix together.
why_en: You can't fix a problem you won't name. Comfort and pizza treat the mood; only brutal, specific facts locate the cause — and a team that helps diagnose will own the cure.
principle_voice_en: If you don't know your numbers, you can't take the right action.

scenario_en: The owner approves your idea for an evening shift to catch after-hours calls — "start whenever you're ready." Calls are being missed nightly, so you're tempted to just put a volunteer rep on the phones Monday and figure it out live.
option_a_en: Build it on paper first: hours, scripts, staffing, bonus, hand-off process, success numbers — then launch.
option_b_en: Launch Monday and adjust as you go — speed beats planning.
option_c_en: Copy a large competitor's after-hours setup exactly.
why_en: Everything is created twice — first in a plan, then in reality. A shift launched without design fails in public, burns the rep, and convinces the owner the idea was bad.
principle_voice_en: If you don't plan your future, it's a pretty good indication you aren't interested in it.

scenario_en: Your newest rep pushes back in training: "Why does the 95% lead-to-appointment standard matter? It's just a quota somebody picked." A couple of veterans look up, curious how you'll answer.
option_a_en: "Because that's the goal management set. Hit it."
option_b_en: Show the why: every lead cost real money and is a family with a wet basement — the standard protects both.
option_c_en: Offer her an extra $5 per set so the number is worth chasing.
why_en: People don't grind for someone else's quota. Connect the number to money already spent and humans waiting for help, and the standard becomes hers. Incentives help, but a why fuels effort no bonus buys.
principle_voice_en: People will not come to work each day fired up to give their best to make you money. There must be something more.

scenario_en: You're the owner. For six years you've personally checked the AC voicemail box at 10pm every night — vacations included. Your spouse is done with it. Your AC manager is capable and has hinted she could own it.
option_a_en: Keep doing it — nobody checks that box like you do.
option_b_en: Compromise: you take weekends, she takes weekdays.
option_c_en: Train her, set a checked-by-9pm standard with a morning report, and hand it over for good.
why_en: A business that can't run an evening without you owns you. Build the standard and the report, transfer the job completely, and the machine finally serves its owner instead of consuming him.
principle_voice_en: Freedom comes when you realize you can't do it alone.

principle_title_en: Do Right When It Costs You
scenario_en: You discover you double-booked tomorrow's confirmed 9am — the salesperson physically can't make it. The customer hasn't noticed. Rescheduling honestly tonight might lose the lead; saying nothing means the salesperson can just show up "running late" somewhere.
option_a_en: Call now, own the mistake, apologize, and offer the two best options plus first claim on any cancellation.
option_b_en: Say nothing; let the salesperson smooth it over tomorrow.
option_c_en: Send an apologetic email tonight offering new times.
why_en: Integrity is what you do when honesty costs an appointment. The cover-up risks the customer, the review, and your culture. A live, honest, generous call usually saves the lead anyway.
principle_voice_en: We don't need upset people out there with Internet connections.

principle_title_en: Hiring Makes You or Breaks You
scenario_en: Two reps quit the same week and the phones are slammed. One applicant responds: she shows up ten minutes late, shrugs through the interview, gives one-word answers — but she has call-center experience and can start tomorrow morning.
option_a_en: Hire her — a warm body now beats an empty chair, and you can always let her go.
option_b_en: Hire her for a "trial week" on overflow calls only.
option_c_en: Keep searching; cover with overtime, shift swaps, and your own hours on the phones.
why_en: The convenient hire answers your phones with a shrug — every shrug costs a paid-for lead. Short-term pain on the schedule beats months of managing a recruiting mistake the customers hear daily.
principle_voice_en: Hiring will make you, or break you.

scenario_en: Final two candidates for an AC seat. One: a call-center veteran with great metrics who bad-mouthed every past employer in the interview. The other: a waitress with zero phone-sales experience who lit up the room and asked smart questions.
option_a_en: Take the veteran — skills pay now; attitude can be coached later.
option_b_en: Hire the waitress and train the skills.
option_c_en: Hire both part-time and keep whoever performs.
why_en: You can teach scripts in weeks; you can't teach warmth or un-teach negativity. The veteran's trash talk about past employers is a preview of your name in her next interview.
principle_voice_en: We don't get people to adopt our core values. We find people who already have them.

scenario_en: Final interview is done. The candidate is... fine. References check out, answers were adequate, nothing wrong — and no spark. The seat has been empty three weeks and the recruiting process would have to restart from zero.
option_a_en: Don't hire; restart the search.
option_b_en: Hire — "fine" plus good training becomes good.
option_c_en: Run a paid trial day and decide afterward.
why_en: If you don't love them in the interview — their best performance — you won't love them on the phones in February. "Fine" hires fill seats and cap departments. The standard is hell yeah.
principle_voice_en: Sometimes the best decisions you ever make are the ones you don't make.

scenario_en: Maria is magic on inbound calls — a born Catcher — but dreads outbound Recycler work, and her cancel-save numbers are awful. Tomas is average on inbound but loves the chase of calling back cancels and old leads. Your current schedule rotates everyone through everything.
option_a_en: Coach Maria harder — everyone on this team must master every role.
option_b_en: Write Maria up for the recycle numbers; standards are standards.
option_c_en: Re-seat them: Maria catches, Tomas recycles — and measure each in their lane.
why_en: The six roles — Catcher, Hunter, Surfer, Recycler, Perennial, Showtime — exist because they need different wiring. Match strengths to seats and both numbers jump; force-fit and you lose Maria and the cancels.
principle_voice_en: Everybody is right for some job.

scenario_en: Jay is 60 days in and still freezes when price-shoppers push him. He's likeable, punctual, and tries hard — but he's only shadowed other reps, never been formally trained, and his set rate is dragging the team average.
option_a_en: Two months is enough runway — let him go.
option_b_en: Build a written plan: daily role-play on price-shoppers, scored calls, a 30-day target — then decide.
option_c_en: Move him permanently off live calls to confirmations.
why_en: Shadowing makes a copy of a copy — that's not training. You owe a willing person a real plan with a real deadline. If he still can't after that, removal is honest, not cruel.
principle_voice_en: Any dummy can buy a truck. Developing the people behind the desk is the key job.

scenario_en: You're the AC manager and the best phone closer in the building. Whenever the board lights up, you jump on calls — and your coaching, scheduling, and recruiting keep sliding to "later." Busy season starts in three weeks and the team still sets at 84%.
option_a_en: Get off the phones except true emergencies; spend the hours training your reps to set like you.
option_b_en: Take the hardest calls yourself — best closer on the toughest leads.
option_c_en: Keep taking calls and do the manager work after hours.
why_en: You're paid for the team's results, not yours. One great closer caps the AC at one person's capacity; a great trainer multiplies it by eight. Heroics on line two is the trap.
principle_voice_en: You don't get paid for your results, but for your team's.

scenario_en: Three weeks ago you handed the show-lead box to Priya with "It's yours now — run with it." Today you discover half the home-show leads were never called. They're going cold, and the owner is asking about show ROI.
option_a_en: Take the box back — clearly it only works when you run it.
option_b_en: Tell Priya she failed and hand it to someone sharper, the same way.
option_c_en: Own the miss: re-delegate with a defined process, daily call target, deadline, and a weekly check-in.
why_en: Handing off a result with no process, goals, or follow-up isn't delegation — it's abdication, and the failure is yours. Same handoff to a new person fails the same way.
principle_voice_en: Deputize — don't surrender ownership.

scenario_en: Your newest rep set only 71% of her leads against the company's 95% standard. You're drafting the write-up when you realize: her onboarding never mentioned the number. Nobody told her. It's posted nowhere. The veterans just "know it."
option_a_en: File the write-up anyway — standards are standards.
option_b_en: Scrap it; set the expectation in writing, train to it, and hold her accountable starting today.
option_c_en: Say nothing and quietly watch one more month for a fair sample.
why_en: Accountability without stated expectations is an ambush. She can't hit a number she's never heard. Set it clearly first; then — and only then — enforcement is fair and effective.
principle_voice_en: If you don't tell your team what you expect, they can't be accountable to it.

scenario_en: Mid-shift, you notice rep Sam just saved his ninth cancelled appointment this week — a department record. He doesn't know you noticed. Payday is two weeks out, the floor is busy, and you have a meeting in ten minutes.
option_a_en: Stop the room now, announce it, and write him a handwritten note he can pin up.
option_b_en: Save it for the monthly meeting so the recognition feels official.
option_c_en: Quietly add $20 to his next check — he'll notice.
why_en: Recognition decays by the hour. Public, immediate, specific praise — plus a handwritten note that lives on a wall for years — beats delayed cash and tells the whole floor what greatness looks like.
principle_voice_en: Every time you talk to someone, you leave them bigger or smaller; the choice is yours.

principle_title_en: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool
scenario_en: Lena, your top rep, has gone flat on calls all week. You learn her mother is in the hospital two towns away. The biggest home-show weekend of the year starts Friday and you were counting on her to anchor the follow-up blitz.
option_a_en: Keep it professional — work is work; remind her how much the show weekend matters.
option_b_en: Quietly schedule her off the blitz and say nothing about why.
option_c_en: Sit with her, ask what she needs, flex her shifts, take something off her plate — and mean it.
why_en: People run through walls for leaders who genuinely care about their lives, not just their numbers. Silent scheduling helps; love out loud builds the loyalty that outlasts ten show weekends.
principle_voice_en: We can't have happy customers without happy, prepared and engaged employees.

principle_title_en: Give Away the Credit, Take the Blame
scenario_en: Your AC just posted its best set month ever — mostly thanks to rep Dee's idea of texting confirmations. At the all-company meeting the owner praises you for the record. Then he asks about a complaint: a family waited two days for a callback because the queue got misrouted. The whole room is watching how you answer both.
option_a_en: Accept the praise graciously and promise to look into the callback complaint.
option_b_en: Redirect the credit to Dee by name, then take the callback miss yourself: "That one's mine — here's the fix."
option_c_en: Call the record "a team effort," and let the rep who misrouted the queue explain the complaint.
why_en: Leaders are megaphones for credit and shock absorbers for blame. Naming Dee builds ten more Dees; owning the miss builds trust. Doing the reverse — even politely — teaches people to hide.
principle_voice_en: Give the credit away; keep the blame.

principle_title_en: Never Act on One Side of a Story
scenario_en: A salesperson storms into the AC: "Your rep Dana sent me to a vacant house this morning — total no-show. Write her up!" Dana is your steadiest rep in three years. The salesperson is standing at your desk, furious, waiting to watch you do something about it right now.
option_a_en: Pull the call recording and CRM notes, hear Dana's side, then decide with full facts.
option_b_en: Write Dana up now — sales is your customer and he's furious.
option_c_en: Defend Dana on the spot and tell him he's exaggerating.
why_en: Incomplete information produces the wrong action almost every time. Maybe the customer lied, maybe the address changed, maybe Dana erred. The recording knows. Acting before you listen punishes someone at random.
principle_voice_en: Half a story produces the wrong action every time.

scenario_en: Your new rep Cole has started answering with a flat "Appointment Center" instead of the smiling scripted greeting — you caught it twice today. His set numbers are still fine, you're buried in the show-lead report, and his 90-day review is only five weeks away. It's a small thing. For now.
option_a_en: Note it in his file as evidence for the 90-day review.
option_b_en: Cover greetings generally at next week's team meeting.
option_c_en: Coach him today — two minutes, replay one recording, reset the standard kindly and clearly.
why_en: Today it's a greeting; in five weeks it's a habit, and by review time it's "how Cole talks." Small problems are cheap to fix only while they're small. The fuse is lit now.
principle_voice_en: When the fuse is lit, that's the moment to act.

principle_title_en: Culture Is When the Boss Leaves
scenario_en: You return from a two-day conference. The phone report from while you were gone: hold times doubled, two leads sat overnight without a first call, and not one Recycler call was made. With you in the room, none of that ever happens. Your first instinct is to find out who slacked.
option_a_en: Install screen monitoring and announce surprise audits whenever you travel.
option_b_en: Read it as your report card: re-teach the why behind each standard, post the numbers daily, and name a floor lead for next time.
option_c_en: Let it go — every team coasts a little when the boss is away.
why_en: What happens when nobody's watching is the culture you actually built. Surveillance rents compliance; understanding the why and owning the scoreboard buys behavior that holds with the lights off.
principle_voice_en: Culture is what your team does when you're not looking.

scenario_en: In the morning huddle, your junior rep raises her hand: "That new closing line we're required to use? Callers go quiet and hang up on me. It feels pushy." The room freezes — everyone knows you wrote that line yourself last month and you're proud of it.
option_a_en: Defend the line — you tested it personally and it works when delivered right.
option_b_en: Say "noted," move on, and quietly think it over later.
option_c_en: Thank her in front of everyone, pull five recordings together this week, and test her wording head-to-head.
why_en: If challenging the boss's idea gets punished — or even just ignored — the room learns to stay silent, and you lose every future warning. Reward the messenger loudly. The best idea wins, not the highest-ranked one.
principle_voice_en: If it's not safe to speak, you'll only hear what you already think.

scenario_en: Friday, 4:55 PM. A salesperson calls in, almost embarrassed: his Monday morning is empty and an empty morning is a paycheck hole. A fresh internet lead just dropped into the queue two minutes ago. Working it properly means staying past close. Monday's rotation would get to it eventually.
option_a_en: Call the lead right now and work it until it's set — salespeople are your customers, and Monday slots feed families.
option_b_en: Leave it for Monday's rotation; it's five minutes to close on a Friday.
option_c_en: Tell him to ask his manager to shuffle another rep's appointments to him.
why_en: The AC's product is a fed sales team. That lead is freshest right now, the need is real, and "Monday" is the convenient choice that quietly starves a teammate. One department, one customer.
principle_voice_en: The Appointment Center keeps the salespeople fed.

principle_title_en: Serve the Human, Not the House
scenario_en: Brutal shift — your last three callers were rude. Now an elderly widow is on the line about water in her basement, but she keeps drifting into stories about her late husband who "always handled these things." Two internet leads are blinking in your queue and your efficiency number is posted on the wall.
option_a_en: Steer her briskly back to the open appointment slots — efficiency serves everyone.
option_b_en: Slow down, smile so she can hear it, listen to the story, then set the appointment at her pace.
option_c_en: Take her number for the callback list so the queue keeps moving.
why_en: She's not buying a drainage system; she's a scared person handling something her husband used to handle. Callers can hear your smile — and your hurry. Serve the human and the appointment sets itself.
principle_voice_en: They can hear your smile through the phone.

scenario_en: A caller says, "You're the third company I've called about my crawl space — and the first actual human who picked up." She's ready to book. You could schedule her in ninety seconds and grab the next ring. Or you could make this call something she tells her neighbors about.
option_a_en: Book the slot efficiently and move on — answering live was already the win.
option_b_en: Mention that the competitors' slow phones probably match their slow service.
option_c_en: Go for Wow: book it, text her confirmation within five minutes, and send the inspector's photo bio and exact arrival window.
why_en: Satisfied customers stay quiet; Wow'd customers talk — and referrals are the cheapest leads you'll ever get. She handed you a moment to be remarkable. "Efficient" is the plausible trap that wastes it.
principle_voice_en: Satisfied customers don't talk. Wow'd ones do.

principle_title_en: The Experience Is Half the Product
scenario_en: You're drafting onboarding for two new hires. A veteran rep reviews your draft and crosses out the tone-and-care module: "We're schedulers. Keep calls short, book the slot — the inspection is what actually sells them." His set rate is decent, and shorter calls do mean more calls per hour.
option_a_en: Teach that the phone call is the customer's first Moment of Truth — tone, their name, genuine care, every single caller.
option_b_en: Adopt his edit — shorter calls mean more calls answered per hour.
option_c_en: Compromise: full care treatment for big-ticket leads, quick handling for the rest.
why_en: The customer starts judging the whole company on ring one — the call IS the product's first half. A cold, fast call poisons the inspection before the inspector's truck even starts.
principle_voice_en: The experience is half of what we sell — and it starts at hello.

scenario_en: Your inspector no-showed a 1:00 PM appointment — truck trouble, his phone died. At 1:25 the homeowner calls in, angry: she took a half-day off work for this. She's mid-sentence about "reading reviews of your competitors tonight." How you handle the next ten minutes is the company to her now.
option_a_en: Explain truthfully what happened to the truck and offer tomorrow's first slot.
option_b_en: Apologize, own it without excuses, and call back inside ten minutes with a same-day arrival — get someone there today.
option_c_en: Escalate it to the sales manager and wait for direction.
why_en: Problems are where customers test who you really are. Explanations feel like excuses to a person who lost a half-day. Speed is the apology — solve it today and she tells the angry story with a happy ending.
principle_voice_en: Speed is the apology.

scenario_en: You inherit the Perennial seat. The customer file holds 1,400 past installs with annual-maintenance dates, but nobody has worked the list in a year — your predecessor "never had time" between live calls. Marketing, meanwhile, is asking for budget to buy more brand-new internet leads at $60 each.
option_a_en: Support the new-lead budget — fresh leads are the lifeblood.
option_b_en: Hand the dusty list to the newest rep as easy practice.
option_c_en: Block daily Perennial hours and call every past customer for their annual check — they're the cheapest, warmest leads the company owns.
why_en: A customer kept for life buys again, refers neighbors, and costs nothing to reach. Letting 1,400 known friends go silent while paying $60 for strangers is the math of a company that forgets people.
principle_voice_en: The sale isn't the end of the relationship — it's the start.

scenario_en: A caller grills you for twenty minutes about wall-crack injection methods, sump pump brands, and warranty fine print. You know your products cold and you're proud of it. He keeps saying, "Just tell me which fix I need and I'll think about calling you back."
option_a_en: Answer warmly but sell the appointment: only a free in-home inspection can diagnose his actual wall — that's the real help.
option_b_en: Demonstrate your expertise: walk him through every method until he trusts you.
option_c_en: Email him the product brochures so he can self-diagnose at his own pace.
why_en: Your product isn't pumps — it's the appointment. Diagnosing a foundation by phone helps no one and risks being wrong. If he hangs up without an inspection, he keeps his problem. Selling the visit IS the helping.
principle_voice_en: Sell the appointment, not the product.

scenario_en: Two leads hit your queue at once. One: an internet form from a lakefront address, full sentences, "finished basement remodel." The other: a shaky voicemail from a rural route, an older voice mentioning "a little water sometimes, if it's not too expensive." You have time to work one perfectly right now.
option_a_en: Work the lakefront lead with your A-game first; squeeze the voicemail in later.
option_b_en: Give both your identical best effort in the order they arrived — book each one fully.
option_c_en: Route the rural voicemail to the newest rep and keep the lakefront lead.
why_en: You can't see bank accounts through a phone line. The "little water" caller may own three paid-off properties; the lakefront form may be a tire-kicker. Cherry-picking is pre-judging — and it trains the whole floor to do it.
principle_voice_en: You never know who you're talking to — so treat everyone like the whale.

scenario_en: A caller is firm: "Just give me a ballpark for waterproofing a basement or I'm hanging up. Everyone hides the price!" You actually know typical job ranges. He sounds genuinely fed up with runaround answers, and you can feel the appointment slipping.
option_a_en: Give a wide honest range so he feels respected, then try to book him.
option_b_en: Quote the low end to get the appointment — the inspector can adjust it later.
option_c_en: Empathize, explain that every basement is different, and offer the free inspection that gets him a real number — not a guess.
why_en: Any phone number is wrong — too high kills the visit, too low blows up in the living room. Price without value has no meaning. Honest empathy plus "a real number, free" books fed-up callers more often than guesses do.
principle_voice_en: A price before value is just a number to say no to.

scenario_en: Quarterly CRM cleanup. You find 212 cancelled and no-show appointments from the past two years sitting in a dead folder. Deleting them takes one click and makes your active pipeline look tidy for tomorrow's owner review. Calling them all would take weeks around your live queue.
option_a_en: Build a Recycler campaign: schedule the whole list, oldest first, fifteen calls a day until every record gets a live answer.
option_b_en: One click — they cancelled for a reason. A clean CRM helps everybody.
option_c_en: Email-blast the list one reactivation coupon, then archive whoever doesn't reply.
why_en: A cancelled appointment is an asset — the problem in their basement didn't cancel. Each record cost real marketing money. The tidy click is the convenient choice that shreds a folder full of paid-for, half-warm leads.
principle_voice_en: They didn't say never — they said not yet.

scenario_en: Month-end. Your lead-to-appointment rate reads 89% against the 95% standard. You trace it: reps have been giving up after one voicemail on internet leads, marking them "unreachable." Each lead cost about $55. Reps say the callbacks "feel like begging" and the live queue keeps them busy anyway.
option_a_en: Accept 89% — it's within shouting distance and the team is genuinely busy.
option_b_en: Show the team the math — 6% missed equals real dollars burned — and install a five-touch minimum before any lead dies.
option_c_en: Ask marketing for cheaper leads so the misses cost less.
why_en: Leads are cash the company already spent. At 89%, you're setting fire to thousands a month one "unreachable" tag at a time. The standard is 95%+ because every point below it is payroll burning.
principle_voice_en: Every lead is money the company already spent — don't leave it on the table.

scenario_en: The owner ties this quarter's AC review to the set-rate number. Your rate would jump from 88% to 96% if you counted only "qualified" leads — quietly excluding wrong numbers, solicitors, and out-of-area calls using your own judgment calls. Other departments, you suspect, already massage their numbers this way.
option_a_en: Use the qualified-only number — it's arguably more accurate anyway.
option_b_en: Report 88% with a written counting standard everyone can audit, plus your plan to raise it honestly.
option_c_en: Report both numbers and let the owner pick which to use.
why_en: A number you can shade is a number you can't steer by. The flattering 96% hides the problem you're paid to fix. Honest counting hurts for one meeting; flying blind hurts every month after.
principle_voice_en: A fudged number is worse than a bad number — you can fix a bad number.

principle_title_en: Pay for What You Want Repeated
scenario_en: You're designing the AC bonus plan. Draft one pays $10 per appointment set, flat. A veteran points out the flaw: reps could book shaky, half-confirmed appointments that no-show on the salesperson — the bonus pays either way. Fixing it means a more complicated plan, and payroll wants it simple by Friday.
option_a_en: Drop the bonus idea entirely — incentives just invite gaming.
option_b_en: Ship the simple plan; your reps are honest people.
option_c_en: Pay on appointments that actually sit — set, confirmed, and showed — so the bonus repeats the behavior you want.
why_en: People do what you pay for, exactly as written — not what you meant. Pay for sets, you'll get sets; pay for sits, you'll get salespeople walking into real living rooms. Design the plan for the behavior, not the hope.
principle_voice_en: Whatever you pay for, you'll get more of — so aim carefully.

scenario_en: Rosa is your AC's superstar — she freestyles every call and sets at 97%. The written script flowchart sits unused in a drawer; nobody else breaks 85%. Rosa just gave notice: she's moving away in three weeks. Panic is setting in about next quarter's numbers.
option_a_en: Sit with Rosa now, mine what she actually says into the script flowchart, and train every rep on the upgraded system before she leaves.
option_b_en: Offer Rosa a big raise to stay remote — protect the 97%.
option_c_en: Recruit hard for "another Rosa" — talent like that is the real answer.
why_en: A department built on a hero dies when the hero leaves. Her magic is just an unwritten system — capture it, and 97% becomes teachable. Predictability is what makes an AC scalable; heroics is what makes it fragile.
principle_voice_en: Build systems so good that ordinary people get extraordinary results.

principle_title_en: How We Do Anything Is How We Do Everything
scenario_en: Friday, 4:50 PM. Last task of the week: logging CRM notes from your final six calls. Nobody reviews Friday notes, the floor is empty, and "spoke w/ cust, set appt" would technically cover it. Monday's salespeople will walk into those houses knowing only whatever you type in the next ten minutes.
option_a_en: Type the quick version — the appointments are set, and that's the part that matters.
option_b_en: Log partial notes now and plan to finish from memory Monday.
option_c_en: Write all six up to full standard — problem described, names, concerns, directions — exactly like Monday-morning notes.
why_en: There is no small version of your standards. The rep who shortcuts unwatched Friday notes shortcuts other things too — and Monday's salesperson walks in blind. Everything counts, especially the things nobody checks.
principle_voice_en: How we do anything is how we do everything.

scenario_en: Your sales team's numbers have slid three months straight. On ride-alongs you notice reps cutting the inspection short and bad-mouthing marketing — the same shortcuts and complaints you've been modeling in Monday meetings. The owner asks you, the sales manager, what's wrong with the team.
option_a_en: Tell the owner the reps have gotten lazy and propose a tougher commission plan.
option_b_en: Say "It starts with me." Fix your own preparation and attitude first, then re-set the standard in person.
option_c_en: Quietly hire two new reps to raise the average.
why_en: The team is the leader's shadow — they copied exactly what you modeled. Different action from you comes before different results from them.
principle_voice_en: You get the team you deserve.

scenario_en: Your mid-pack rep storms in: "Marketing keeps feeding me junk leads. Give me the good zip codes and I'll close like Marcus does." The CRM shows he and Marcus draw from the same randomized lead pool — but Marcus banks nearly four times the dollars per lead.
option_a_en: Agree the leads look weak and lobby marketing for "better" ones.
option_b_en: Move him to the wealthiest zip codes for a month to test his theory.
option_c_en: Show him the numbers: same pool, different results. Coach the real variable — the salesperson.
why_en: The same ten leads made Lowman $11,000 and Highman $54,300. Blaming the leads is the loser's pattern; owning the result is where improvement starts.
principle_voice_en: Everything happens for a reason. Change the reasons and you change what happens.

scenario_en: You lost three closes in one brutal week — one customer laughed at your price. Tomorrow you have two fresh appointments, and tonight you're tempted to coast, skip practice, and "protect your confidence" by playing it safe on price.
option_a_en: Write down what each "no" taught you, rehearse the fix tonight, and run tomorrow's leads at full enthusiasm.
option_b_en: Take a few days off to let your confidence recover.
option_c_en: Quietly quote lower on the next call so you don't get rejected again.
why_en: Rejection costs you nothing you had. Turned into study and practice, it becomes fuel; turned into price-cutting fear, it becomes poison that follows you everywhere.
principle_voice_en: Your pain can be your poison or your fuel – you choose.

scenario_en: You're the sales manager planning next quarter's meetings. Your veteran says role play is "for rookies," and nobody has done a ride-along in a year. Meanwhile the bottom half of the board hasn't improved in two quarters.
option_a_en: Excuse veterans from role play to keep the peace; require it for rookies only.
option_b_en: Buy everyone an online sales course to watch at home.
option_c_en: Run weekly role play for everyone — veterans first — plus regular ride-alongs, coaching by appreciation.
why_en: Skill grows through repetition with feedback, not seniority. When the best players practice first, practice becomes the culture instead of a punishment.
principle_voice_en: What's easy to do is easy not to do.

scenario_en: It's 8 PM. The inspection went great and the homeowners are leaning in. You're tired, and emailing a "polished proposal in a few days" sounds professional — and easier. You know your company standard: same-day proposal, full process, three asks.
option_a_en: Promise a beautifully formatted proposal by Friday — it looks more professional.
option_b_en: Build the proposal now, present it, and ask for the order — up to three times — before you leave.
option_c_en: Leave a brochure and a price range; follow up next week.
why_en: The value and excitement you built drop like a rock the moment you leave. The basics — same-day proposal, full process, three asks — are where the battle is won.
principle_voice_en: Become brilliant on the basics, because that is where the battle is won or lost.

scenario_en: Forecast meeting tomorrow. Your pipeline is stuffed with deals that haven't responded in months, making the quarter look safe. The owner is about to approve hiring based on your number. Scrubbing it honestly will make you look behind.
option_a_en: Scrub the pipeline to truth — dead deals out, real stages, real dates — and present the honest gap with a plan.
option_b_en: Leave it inflated; big numbers keep everyone motivated.
option_c_en: Trim a little, but keep the big stale deal the owner loves asking about.
why_en: You can't chart a course from a position you faked. Decisions built on an inflated pipeline fail; an honest gap plus a plan builds trust and action.
principle_voice_en: Our wisdom is as much illusions lost as knowledge acquired.

scenario_en: Tomorrow night you run the biggest referral lead of your year — a finished-basement prospect referred by your best customer. Your rapport is strong and you're tempted to just show up and let the conversation flow.
option_a_en: Wing it — rapport is your gift, and scripts feel stiff.
option_b_en: Skim the lead sheet for two minutes in their driveway.
option_c_en: Plan it the day before: study the home and referral notes, set call objectives, rehearse your Agenda and likely objections.
why_en: Everything is created twice — once in your mind, once in the living room. A call planned in detail the day before runs itself; a winged call wanders.
principle_voice_en: You have to have a dream to make a dream come true.

scenario_en: The homeowner says she wants the foundation crack fixed "before we list the house someday." But twice she mentions her daughter's allergies and won't let the kids play in the musty downstairs room. The cheap crack patch is the easy quote.
option_a_en: Quote the simple crack repair she asked for and head out.
option_b_en: Keep asking questions until the real why surfaces, then build the Accomplish List around her family's health and that room.
option_c_en: Pitch the full system immediately — you can sense the bigger need.
why_en: Reasons come first, answers second. When the solution connects to her real why — her kids — the decision gets easy and the job gets right-sized.
principle_voice_en: If there is no why, the how doesn't matter.

scenario_en: You own the company and still run every sales lead yourself — nights, weekends, missed ballgames. Your closing ratio is the best in the shop, and you tell yourself nobody can sell like you. Your spouse stopped asking when you'll be home.
option_a_en: Hire and train a salesperson, hand off leads with a real system, and keep the owner's job: building the team.
option_b_en: Keep selling everything yourself — your closing ratio pays the bills.
option_c_en: Raise prices so you can run fewer leads personally.
why_en: A business is supposed to serve its owner, not consume him. Your winning strategy of working harder has become your losing strategy — it doesn't scale and it's eating your life.
principle_voice_en: You want your business to give you more of a life, not take more of your life.

principle_title_en: Do Right When It Costs You
scenario_en: Your neighbor wants the same waterproofing system you sell every day and hints at a "friend price." You could under-measure the perimeter a little, or just not report the proposal so nobody asks questions. He's standing in your driveway waiting.
option_a_en: Give a small unofficial discount — he's your neighbor, after all.
option_b_en: Under-measure slightly; nobody ever checks the linear footage.
option_c_en: Quote the standard price, measure true, and report the proposal like every other one.
why_en: One price list, no games — and hidden activity always gets discovered. Integrity that bends for a neighbor will bend for anyone, and the team learns from what you do.
principle_voice_en: Everyone gets the same price — uptown, downtown, east side and west side.

principle_title_en: Hiring Makes You or Breaks You
scenario_en: Busy season starts in six weeks and you're one rep short. Today's applicant has a pulse, a license, and not much else. Every week the seat stays empty, leads pile up — and you're the one running them after hours.
option_a_en: Hire him today; the leads are burning and a body beats a hole.
option_b_en: Keep the bar high — interview like it's your third-ever hire, work your bench of employed prospects, absorb leads short-term.
option_c_en: Hire him as a "trial run" and decide later.
why_en: A wrong sales hire burns leads, reputation, and months of training time — far more than an empty seat costs. Show the same care hiring your 73rd employee as your 3rd.
principle_voice_en: In 30 years I have never regretted firing someone (although I have regretted hiring many of the wrong people!)

scenario_en: A top producer from your biggest competitor applies. His numbers are dazzling. Two reference calls hint at the same thing: side deals and fudged paperwork. Your team would learn a lot from his closing skills — and maybe a few other things.
option_a_en: Pass. Skills can be trained into honest people; honesty can't be trained into skilled ones.
option_b_en: Hire him with "tight monitoring" and strict paperwork audits.
option_c_en: Hire him and pair him with your most ethical veteran so the good rubs off.
why_en: Whatever he games will spread, because top producers set the tone. If people don't believe the messenger, they won't believe the message — and customers will eventually find out.
principle_voice_en: If people don't believe the messenger, they won't believe the message.

scenario_en: Final interview. The candidate is a level-10 talent — sharp, experienced, magnetic. When you ask why he wants this job, he shrugs: "I figured I could try it for a while and see." Your gut sinks, but the talent is rare.
option_a_en: Sweeten the offer until his enthusiasm appears.
option_b_en: Hire him — talent that rare is worth the gamble.
option_c_en: Pass. A level-7 who wants to be here beats a level-10 who isn't sure.
why_en: Don't settle for "maybe." Lukewarm talent quits in your busiest month, after eating your best leads. Desire is the fuel that talent runs on.
principle_voice_en: Desire is talent seeking expression.

scenario_en: Your best inside scheduler begged for outside sales. Three months in he's miserable and far below quota — but he's still gold on the phone, rescuing cancelled appointments nobody else can save. He's embarrassed to go back; you're embarrassed to move him.
option_a_en: Move him into the Recycler seat where his phone talent wins — with dignity, a clear plan, and a real path.
option_b_en: Let him go; he failed at sales.
option_c_en: Give outside sales six more months — moving him now looks like quitting.
why_en: One personality is ideal for one job and not another. The failure was the seat, not the person — and a rescued appointment is worth as much as a closed door knock.
principle_voice_en: One personality is ideal for one job and not another.

scenario_en: In meetings, every rep nods along with the new presentation. But the CRM and ride-alongs show nobody actually uses it, and the mid-pack keeps slipping. They're "yes-ing" you in the room and hiding in the field.
option_a_en: Accept it — veterans have earned their own style.
option_b_en: Make role play weekly and non-optional, coach each rep individually, and remove anyone who won't respond to real training.
option_c_en: Send a firm memo re-requiring the new presentation.
why_en: A sales team that doesn't role play will "yes" you and hide. Either train people to better or remove them — hope is not a strategy, and tolerated mediocrity multiplies.
principle_voice_en: An environment that doesn't like mediocrity but accepts it gets mediocrity.

scenario_en: You're the sales manager, and you still keep the juiciest leads for yourself. Your personal number shines; your reps stagnate, and two have quietly asked why the best opportunities never reach them. Training time keeps getting bumped for your appointments.
option_a_en: Keep closing — the company needs your revenue.
option_b_en: Keep only the biggest, toughest jobs and distribute the rest.
option_c_en: Hand off all the leads. Your job is building sellers: recruiting, training, ride-alongs, and meetings.
