why_en: Every hour you sell, nobody is building the team — and the team is the only thing that scales. The manager who out-sells his reps has the wrong scoreboard.
principle_voice_en: What got you here, won't get you there.

scenario_en: You handed your new rep the entire unsold-proposal pool with a cheerful "go get 'em" — no system, no targets, no check-ins. One bad week later you're about to yank it all back and work it yourself.
option_a_en: Define the result you expect, train her on the follow-up system, set weekly check-ins, and let her run it.
option_b_en: Take the pool back — it's faster to do it yourself.
option_c_en: Leave her completely alone; she'll figure it out or she won't.
why_en: Dumping work with no expectations isn't delegation, and snatching it back isn't management. Delegate the authority and the method, keep the responsibility and the check-ins.
principle_voice_en: Delegate authority, retain responsibility.

scenario_en: Your new rep is three weeks in. You're about to write him up for low dollars-per-lead and skipping same-day proposals — then it hits you: nobody ever told him the ADL target or that same-day proposals are the standard here.
option_a_en: Write him up anyway; those standards are obvious in sales.
option_b_en: Sit down first: explicit ADL target, full process expectations, in writing, agreed — then hold him accountable to them.
option_c_en: Skip the talk and just post his numbers on the public board.
why_en: You can't hold people accountable to expectations you never set. Make the standard explicit and agreed first; accountability without expectations is just ambush.
principle_voice_en: Expectation gaps lead to execution gaps... There is not a close second.

scenario_en: Your perennial bottom rep tops the sales board for one week — his first time ever. The veterans roll their eyes: "One hot week." Monday's meeting agenda is already full, and you could just nod at him in the hallway.
option_a_en: Say nothing — one week proves nothing.
option_b_en: Privately warn him not to slide back now that he's shown he can do it.
option_c_en: Celebrate it loudly in the meeting — name it, clap for it, let him feel like a winner in front of everyone.
why_en: Salespeople must see themselves as winners; commission and confidence feed each other in a loop. Celebrating the bottom rep's win pulls the whole bottom of the board upward.
principle_voice_en: Pretend every employee has a sign around their neck that says, 'Make me feel important.

principle_title_en: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool
scenario_en: Peak season, board on fire — and your top closer's wife just landed in the hospital. He insists he'll keep running his leads: "We need the numbers." The whole team is watching what you do next.
option_a_en: Cover his leads, send him to the hospital with pay, and check on him yourself — the team sees how you treat people.
option_b_en: Let him keep working; he asked to, and adults decide for themselves.
option_c_en: Thank him for the commitment and quietly book him double — the season is short.
why_en: People know if you really care, and soldiers fight for leaders who love them. One season's leads are cheap; a team that knows you'd cover for them is priceless.
principle_voice_en: In the end it comes down to: Do you love people?

principle_title_en: Give Away the Credit, Take the Blame
scenario_en: You're the sales manager. The quarter closed at a record, largely on a referral push your rookie rep Ana invented. At the company dinner the owner toasts "your brilliant quarter." He also asks why a big commercial proposal blew up last month — it died because you sat on the paperwork for a week.
option_a_en: Accept the toast for the team and explain the commercial deal hit "process delays."
option_b_en: Smile through the toast, then privately thank Ana later tonight.
option_c_en: Stand up, name Ana and her referral idea as the reason, then own the dead deal yourself: "I sat on it. My fix: 48-hour paperwork."
why_en: Credit given away multiplies — Ana will invent three more ideas, and the team learns initiative pays. Blame absorbed builds trust. "Process delays" is just blame wearing a tie.
principle_voice_en: Pass the praise down, pull the blame up.

principle_title_en: Never Act on One Side of a Story
scenario_en: A homeowner calls the office in tears: your rep Victor "pressured her for two hours and wouldn't leave." Victor is your top closer with a thick referral file. The owner forwards you the complaint with one line: "Handle this today." You haven't talked to Victor yet; he's mid-appointment across town.
option_a_en: Call the customer first to apologize and promise Victor will be disciplined.
option_b_en: Get both sides today: call her back with care, then sit with Victor, check appointment notes and times, and decide on facts.
option_c_en: Back Victor — top closers attract complaints; it comes with the job.
why_en: Incomplete information produces wrong action. Maybe Victor crossed a line; maybe she's price-shocked and rewriting the visit. Promising discipline before facts betrays Victor; dismissing her betrays the customer. Hear both, then act.
principle_voice_en: One side of a story is a coin flip dressed up as a decision.

scenario_en: Reviewing CRM timestamps, you notice your steady mid-pack rep has started arriving 10-15 minutes late to appointments — three times in two weeks. His close rate hasn't dipped yet, he's a nice guy, and you hate awkward conversations. The monthly one-on-one is seventeen days away.
option_a_en: Talk to him today — brief, friendly, direct: late arrivals end now, and ask what's behind them.
option_b_en: Wait for the one-on-one; three data points isn't a pattern yet.
option_c_en: Send the whole team a reminder email about punctuality.
why_en: Late is a lit fuse: today it's minutes, next month it's no-shows and one-star reviews. The team email punishes nineteen innocent people and warns the guilty one nothing. Small, now, kind — that's cheap. Later is expensive.
principle_voice_en: Problems are puppies — train them small or fight them grown.

principle_title_en: Culture Is When the Boss Leaves
scenario_en: You take your first real vacation in three years. Back Monday, you check the CRM: while you were gone, same-day proposals dropped from 90% to 40%, two reps quoted "ballparks" by phone, and Friday's sales meeting was cancelled "since you weren't here to run it."
option_a_en: Cancel future vacations — clearly the place needs you in the room.
option_b_en: Call out the slackers individually; the rest don't need a lecture.
option_c_en: Treat it as your grade, not theirs: rebuild the whys behind each standard, and train a rep to run meetings whether you're there or not.
why_en: What your team does unwatched is what you actually taught. If standards live only in your presence, you built supervision, not culture — and a department that can't survive a vacation can't survive growth.
principle_voice_en: The real culture report runs while you're at the beach.

scenario_en: Sales meeting. You unveil the new proposal template you spent your weekend building. A second-year rep says, "Honestly? Page three confuses customers — I watched two of them glaze over this week." A veteran snorts at her. Everyone looks at you, the author, to see what happens to people who do that.
option_a_en: Note the feedback but ship the template as-is; one rep's anecdote isn't data.
option_b_en: Thank her publicly, shut down the snort, and ask the room to test page three on next week's calls and report back.
option_c_en: Discuss it with her one-on-one after the meeting so the rollout isn't undermined.
why_en: The room just ran a test: is truth welcome here? Sidebar conversations protect your ego, not the team — everyone saw the snort win. Reward the messenger in public and the best idea starts beating the highest rank.
principle_voice_en: Shoot one messenger and you've silenced a hundred.

scenario_en: You close a tricky crawl space job at 7 PM — barely. To get the signature you verbally promised "they can probably start Thursday" and waved off the customer's question about the cluttered access hatch: "The crew handles all that." Now you're writing up the job packet, tired, and the details feel optional.
option_a_en: Write the full truth into the packet: the Thursday promise, the blocked hatch, photos, measurements — then call production tomorrow to align before the customer hears anything.
option_b_en: Submit the standard packet; production always figures out site conditions on arrival.
option_c_en: Note the hatch but leave out the Thursday comment — it was only a "probably."
why_en: Production is your customer, and you just sold them a job with a hidden promise and a hidden obstacle. Setting them up to win is the second half of your sale; a surprised crew becomes an angry customer with your name on it.
principle_voice_en: Sales writes the check that production has to cash.

principle_title_en: Serve the Human, Not the House
scenario_en: Tonight's appointment: an engineer who answers the door with a spreadsheet of foundation-repair methods and three competitor quotes. Your standard presentation is warm, story-driven, and full of family photos. Last week the same deck wowed a chatty retired couple for forty-five minutes. He checks his watch as you unzip your bag.
option_a_en: Run your proven presentation — it's a system, and systems work when you do them the same every time.
option_b_en: Skip the presentation entirely and just talk numbers like he wants.
option_c_en: Flex the style, keep the process: lead with data, specs, and direct answers — every step still done, delivered the way HE buys.
why_en: Four personality styles buy four different ways; the Platinum Rule says treat them how THEY want to be treated. The steps don't change — the delivery does. Stories for the storyteller, specs for the engineer.
principle_voice_en: Sell to the person in front of you, not the one from last week.

scenario_en: Mid-inspection, the homeowner mentions her sump pump discharge line freezes every winter — not your job, not in your quote, a ten-minute fix with a $15 part. You're running tight to your next appointment, and the deal you came for is basically closed already.
option_a_en: Recommend a handyman for the discharge line and wrap up.
option_b_en: Fix it on the spot — or have it handled free with the install — and point it out without being asked twice.
option_c_en: Add the discharge fix to the proposal as a $95 line item.
why_en: Satisfied customers are silent; Wow'd customers tell neighbors, write reviews, and refer. A $15 part and ten minutes buys the story she'll tell for years — that flywheel of referrals is the cheapest marketing that exists.
principle_voice_en: Wow isn't extra — Wow is the job.

principle_title_en: The Experience Is Half the Product
scenario_en: Heat wave, 4:45 PM, last appointment of the day. You're tempted to skip the confirmation call ("they know I'm coming"), leave the wrinkled logo shirt in the truck for the comfortable t-shirt, and drop the printed Agenda — "folks find it stiff anyway." Your product knowledge will carry it. It always has.
option_a_en: Confirm anyway, change into the clean logo shirt, arrive on the minute, and open with the Agenda — full standard, last call of the day.
option_b_en: Skip just the Agenda; the call and the shirt are the parts customers actually notice.
option_c_en: Show up comfortable and friendly — authenticity sells better than costumes.
why_en: The customer can't see your product's quality buried in a wall — they judge it by what they CAN see: your shirt, your punctuality, your confirmation, your Agenda. The experience is half of what they're buying.
principle_voice_en: They can't see the product — so the experience IS the product.

scenario_en: Saturday morning. Last week's customer calls your cell, upset: the crew finished yesterday and left muddy bootprints across her new carpet — and a gate open, letting her dog loose for an hour. The dog's fine. Production's office opens Monday. It wasn't your crew, and it's your kid's soccer day.
option_a_en: Apologize and promise production will call her first thing Monday.
option_b_en: Explain that installation issues go through the production line, and text her that number.
option_c_en: Own it now: apologize as the company, arrange carpet cleaning today, and follow up in person Monday — speed is the apology.
why_en: She didn't buy from "production" — she bought from you. Problems are the test that turns customers into critics or evangelists, and the grade is mostly speed. Handled today, this becomes the story she tells in your favor.
principle_voice_en: Customers forgive problems; they never forgive slow.

scenario_en: Your install from last month is done, paid, and closed out. The post-install callback, review request, and referral ask are on your list — but so are five hot new appointments this week, and the commission on a closed file is already spent. Calling finished customers earns you nothing this pay period.
option_a_en: Skip it — happy customers call you if something's wrong.
option_b_en: Make the callback this week: confirm she's thrilled, ask for the review, ask who else on her street has water issues.
option_c_en: Have the office send her an automated satisfaction survey.
why_en: A customer kept for life is a referral engine, a review, and a repeat buyer — the most profitable "lead" you'll ever work. The callback costs ten minutes and pays for years. Closed-and-forgotten is how companies stay small.
principle_voice_en: The cheapest customer to win is the one you already won.

scenario_en: The inspection is clear: this crawl space needs full encapsulation or the rot keeps spreading into the floor joists. The homeowner winces at the number and offers you an exit: "Maybe we just do nothing for now — it's been like this for years, right?" Agreeing would be comfortable, and you'd still part friends.
option_a_en: Respectfully stay: show him the rot photos again, connect it to his sagging floor, and ask for the order — walking away leaves him with the problem.
option_b_en: Honor his choice immediately — pushing past a "no" is what gives sales a bad name.
option_c_en: Offer to cut the scope in half so the price stops scaring him.
why_en: If you don't sell him the solution, he keeps the problem — and the rot doesn't pause while he thinks. Backing off feels polite but abandons him to a worsening house. Persisting with evidence and care IS the helping.
principle_voice_en: When you fail to sell them, they keep their problem.

scenario_en: Tomorrow's lead sheet: a single-wide mobile home on the far edge of your territory, forty minutes out, "musty smell under the house." Your buddy on the team laughs: "That's a $200 dehumidifier sale, max. Swap it for my Thursday cancellation list and save the gas." You've spent enough wallet-projection lessons to feel the itch anyway.
option_a_en: Run it, but bring only the small-job options to keep the visit quick.
option_b_en: Swap with your buddy — territory time is money, and the math favors Thursday.
option_c_en: Run it with the full inspection, full presentation, and the complete solution priced — same as a lakefront house.
why_en: You can't see savings accounts from the driveway. Some of the biggest jobs in company history came from "small" houses — and your wallet is not their wallet. Pre-qualifying with your eyes is how whales swim away.
principle_voice_en: Don't project your wallet onto their decision.

scenario_en: Two minutes inside the door, before you've seen the basement, the husband crosses his arms: "We've had three quotes. Just give us your number and we'll tell you if it's worth your time to do the dog-and-pony show." His wife already has a notepad out with three figures on it.
option_a_en: Give a rough range — refusing will read as evasive against three competitors who quoted.
option_b_en: Smile, agree his time matters, and explain you quote real numbers, not guesses — earn the inspection, build the Accomplish List, then price.
option_c_en: Beat their lowest written number to cut through the comparison.
why_en: A price before value is just a big scary number — without the gap between what they have and what they could have, every figure loses to the cheapest quote. No ballparks: the process is what makes the number make sense.
principle_voice_en: Price without value always sounds expensive.

scenario_en: New CRM rollout next week, and you're told to migrate only "active" proposals. Your unsold list holds 67 names — some eight months old, some who said "maybe in spring," some who went silent. Migrating them all means tagging each one by hand tonight. Marking them "closed-lost" takes one batch click.
option_a_en: Migrate every unsold proposal with a next-contact date on each — the pool is gold, and spring always comes.
option_b_en: Batch-close the list — eight months of silence is an answer.
option_c_en: Keep the ten newest and close the rest; focus beats clutter.
why_en: Until the sale is made, the lead is alive — their wet basement didn't close itself. People buy when their life is ready, not when your CRM is tidy. The batch click is the convenient choice that deletes next year's commissions.
principle_voice_en: Follow up until they buy or die.

scenario_en: End of a long appointment, the deal is verbally won at $14,800. The couple looks tired. Mentioning the deposit and walking through financing options means another fifteen minutes and a flicker of risk — they could waver. You could just shake hands, skip the money talk, and "let the office sort out payment this week."
option_a_en: Take the signature tonight, collect the deposit, and present financing options like you do every time — payment is part of the close.
option_b_en: Sign tonight, collect the deposit, but skip financing — they didn't ask, and it muddies a done deal.
option_c_en: Shake hands warmly and have the office handle deposit and payment this week.
why_en: A sale isn't a sale until money moves — deposits make decisions real, and unfinanced sticker shock kills "done" deals by Thursday. Offer financing every time: most objections are money objections wearing a costume.
principle_voice_en: All objections are money objections — so solve the money.

scenario_en: Quarterly review tomorrow, ranked by ADL — average dollars per lead. Yours sags because of six brutal no-sale leads in March. A teammate shows you the trick: recode no-shows and "bad" leads as "unqualified" and they drop out of your denominator. "Everyone massages it," he shrugs. Your ranking would jump four spots overnight.
option_a_en: Recode only the two genuinely hopeless ones — that's just accuracy.
option_b_en: Report every lead you ran, take the honest ADL, and bring your plan to raise it.
option_c_en: Recode like everyone else — a level playing field requires the same math.
why_en: ADL is the one number that tells the truth about a salesperson — but only if the denominator is honest. Shrink it and you're not ranked higher, you're just lied to. You can't improve a number you've rigged.
principle_voice_en: ADL doesn't lie — unless you make it.

principle_title_en: Pay for What You Want Repeated
scenario_en: You're redesigning the sales pay plan. The old plan paid pure commission on gross sales — and bred ugly habits: overselling jobs that later got trimmed, fighting over big leads, zero follow-up on small ones. The reps like the old plan; the loudest veteran says, "Don't fix what pays."
option_a_en: Build the plan around what you want repeated — sold-and-installed revenue, follow-up worked, customer reviews — and walk the team through the why.
option_b_en: Keep the old plan but add a quarterly bonus for "good behavior" at your discretion.
option_c_en: Keep pure gross commission; simple plans cause the fewest arguments.
why_en: A pay plan is your loudest, most permanent instruction — people repeat exactly what it pays for, including the ugly parts. Pay on installed revenue and worked follow-up, and the gaming dies because gaming stops paying.
principle_voice_en: Show me the pay plan and I'll show you the behavior.

scenario_en: Your closer Drew sells almost double the team average — by improvising. He skips the Agenda, eyeballs measurements, prices "by feel," reorders the steps every call. It works for Drew. Two rookies now copy his shortcuts without his instincts, and their numbers are cratering. Drew says the process is "training wheels."
option_a_en: Let Drew freelance — results buy freedom — but make the rookies follow the process.
option_b_en: Split the difference: a "lite" process for anyone above quota.
option_c_en: One process, in order, every call, everyone — and channel Drew's genius into improving the system itself, not escaping it.
why_en: A company of heroes isn't a company — it's a bet that never scales and dies when Drew leaves. Predictability is what makes growth possible. Put his magic INTO the process and every rookie inherits it.
principle_voice_en: Heroes win calls; systems win companies.

principle_title_en: How We Do Anything Is How We Do Everything
scenario_en: Last appointment ran short — the customer signed in forty minutes. You're home by 8 with one task left: tonight's call report and tomorrow's pre-call planning sheets. Nobody audits these. You closed today; you're clearly sharp. The couch and the game are right there, and "I'll do them at the coffee shop tomorrow" has worked before.
option_a_en: Skip the paperwork as a reward — performance earned the night off.
option_b_en: Do it all now, at full standard, tonight — the report, both planning sheets, every field — like every other night.
option_c_en: Knock out the call report tonight and wing tomorrow's planning at the first red light.
why_en: There are no small exceptions — every shortcut votes for who you are. The discipline that holds when no one checks and nothing is at stake is the same discipline that shows up at the close. Everything counts.
principle_voice_en: There's no off-duty version of your standards.

scenario_en: You're the production manager. For a month you've rolled into the yard at 7:20 for a 7:00 dispatch, coffee in hand, returning texts. Now two crews are loading late, one foreman skipped his truck check, and jobs are starting an hour behind. The owner asks why mornings have gotten sloppy. You honestly don't know where it started.
option_a_en: Post a memo: anyone not loading by 7:05 loses Friday overtime priority.
option_b_en: Hold a crew meeting on punctuality and ask the foremen to police each other.
option_c_en: Be at the gate at 6:45 every day yourself for a month, then re-look at the crews.
why_en: The department reflects its leader. The sloppiness started with you, so the fix starts with you. Rules and meetings can't out-shout your example.
principle_voice_en: We build a better business by building a better person in the leader. It's the only way it can be done.

scenario_en: Your newest installer set a sump basin out of level and the slab has to be chipped out — a $2,200 redo. He was on your crew for three weeks. You showed him the basin install once, on a day you were rushing to beat rain. The owner asks what happened. Your foreman bonus takes the hit either way.
option_a_en: Report it straight: the kid was trained and still missed it; write him up.
option_b_en: Tell the owner: "I trained him in one rushed pass. That's on me. Here's my retraining plan."
option_c_en: Split the difference — note he's green, ask the owner to waive the bonus hit this once.
why_en: You hired him onto the task, you trained him, you set the standard. Total responsibility is the only position that gives you the power to fix it.
principle_voice_en: Whatever your organization is today, ask 'How did I cause this?

scenario_en: The county inspector just failed your footing inspection — wrong rebar spacing — in front of the homeowner. It's your first fail in two years and the redo eats the weekend. Back in the truck, your helper says, "That guy had it out for us." You're embarrassed and angry, and Monday's crew meeting is yours to run.
option_a_en: Open Monday's meeting with the fail, what YOU missed, and a new rebar checklist for every footing.
option_b_en: Let it go quietly — fix the spacing, don't broadcast a one-off embarrassment to the crew.
option_c_en: Tell the crew the inspector is picky in that township, so double-check spacing there.
why_en: Setbacks are poison or fuel — you choose. Blaming the inspector or hiding the fail changes nothing. Changing the inputs (a checklist, a public lesson) turns pain into a system.
principle_voice_en: Your pain can be your poison or your fuel – you choose.

scenario_en: You're a foreman with ninety minutes of windshield time daily. The company offers to load the truck with trade audio and pay for a waterproofing certification course — two evenings a week for six weeks, during softball season. Your installs pass inspection fine already, and nobody else on the crew is signing up. The production manager says it's optional.
option_a_en: Pass this round — you're already passing inspections, and evenings are family time.
option_b_en: Do the audio only — free learning without giving up evenings.
option_c_en: Take the course and the audio — work harder on yourself than on your job.
why_en: "Good enough already" is how people get stale and cap out. The certification compounds: better pay, bigger jobs, foreman-of-foremen track. Easy to skip — which is exactly why most skip it.
principle_voice_en: What's easy to do is easy not to do.

scenario_en: Friday, 4:40 p.m., a simple two-day crawl-space job is done and the customer seems happy. Your company's close-out basics: final walk-through with the homeowner, broom-clean the work area, photos, collect payment, ask for referrals. The crew wants to beat traffic, and the homeowner says, "Don't worry about the walk-through, it looks great."
option_a_en: Skip the walk-through since she waived it; do photos and payment, head out.
option_b_en: Run the full close-out anyway — walk-through, cleanup, photos, payment, referral ask. Traffic waits.
option_c_en: Do the walk-through but skip photos and the referral ask — she's clearly already sold.
why_en: The basics work only when they're done without fail. "She waived it" is how callbacks, missed punch items, and unasked referrals happen. Easy to do, easy not to do.
principle_voice_en: Become brilliant on the basics, because that is where the battle is won or lost.

scenario_en: You're the production manager. The schedule board says you're booked five weeks out — looks great. But you know two of those jobs have unsigned change orders, one customer hasn't paid a deposit, and a crew lead just gave notice. The owner is about to approve a big material order and a new hire based on that board.
option_a_en: Let the order ride — the board usually works itself out and you hate looking alarmist.
option_b_en: Re-build the board to show only confirmed, deposited, crewed work, then walk the owner through the true picture today.
option_c_en: Flag the crew-lead gap, the most urgent piece, and handle the soft jobs as they surface.
why_en: Decisions made on a fiction become expensive facts. To set things right you have to see things right — backlog counts only when it's signed, funded, and crewed.
principle_voice_en: To set things right, you have to see things right.

scenario_en: Monday you start your biggest job of the year: a $54,000 full-perimeter system with an egress window, two crews, a pump rental, and an inspection sequence you've never run in this township. You could spend Friday afternoon building a day-by-day job plan — or use Friday to knock out a small punch-list job that's nagging you.
option_a_en: Spend Friday planning: sequence, inspections, deliveries, crew assignments, drawn out day by day.
option_b_en: Knock out the punch list — you've run big jobs before; plan it Sunday night from memory.
option_c_en: Plan the first two days in detail and figure the rest as conditions emerge.
why_en: Everything is created twice — first in the mind, then in concrete. A $54,000 job with an unfamiliar inspection sequence built "as you go" gets built twice in reality instead.
principle_voice_en: You have to have a dream to make a dream come true.

scenario_en: Corporate rolls out a new rule: every foreman shoots five job photos daily and texts a one-line status to the office. Your crews grumble — "more babysitting." You're the production manager introducing it at the Monday meeting. You have ten minutes and a room full of guys who hate paperwork.
option_a_en: Keep it short: "New policy, five photos a day, non-negotiable, starting today."
option_b_en: Soften it: "Office wants photos — just do your best when you remember."
option_c_en: Show how photos killed a $9,000 false damage claim last year, win marketing leads, and prove crew quality — then the rule.
why_en: Reasons first, answers second. Crews who know photos protect their own work and their bonuses comply without policing. A rule without a why becomes optional the day you're not looking.
principle_voice_en: If there is no why, the how doesn't matter.

scenario_en: You're the production manager and you haven't had a full Saturday off since March. You personally open the shop, run dispatch, and ride to every tricky job. Your daughter's championship game is Saturday. There's a routine install scheduled — a job your senior foreman has done thirty times. Old habit says be there anyway.
option_a_en: Brief the senior foreman Friday, give him the dispatch keys, go to the game with your phone on for true emergencies.
option_b_en: Go to the game but call the foreman every two hours for status.
option_c_en: Catch the first half, then swing by the job — best of both.
why_en: The job exists to give you more of a life, not take more of it. A routine job your best foreman has done thirty times is exactly what you built him for.
principle_voice_en: You want your business to give you more of a life, not take more of your life.

principle_title_en: Do Right When It Costs You
scenario_en: Demo day on a finished-basement job, your crew finds active termite damage in a sill plate — hidden behind paneling, outside your contract scope. Telling the customer means a stop, a treatment contractor, and probably losing your schedule slot; your install bonus slides a month. The paneling goes back up either way, and nobody would ever know.
option_a_en: Photograph it and note it in the file, mention it casually at close-out so the schedule holds.
option_b_en: Stop, show the homeowner the damage today, explain options, and reschedule around the treatment.
option_c_en: Close it up — it's outside scope, and you're not a termite inspector.
why_en: If you discover hidden problems, the customer has to know — now, not at close-out. Doing right when it costs you a bonus is the only time "doing right" means anything.
principle_voice_en: Never look the other way — if you discover hidden problems on a job, the customer has to know.

principle_title_en: Hiring Makes You or Breaks You
scenario_en: You're down one installer with a six-week backlog. A walk-in applies: he has tools, can start Monday, but his last two jobs lasted under four months and his references aren't calling back. Your other option is to run crews short for two or three more weeks while you keep recruiting, paying overtime you'll feel in job costs.
option_a_en: Hire him for a "trial week" — low risk, and you need the hands.
option_b_en: Pass on hiring, and quietly borrow a helper from your buddy's roofing crew off the books.
option_c_en: Run short, pay the overtime, and keep recruiting until references and history check out on someone.
why_en: 95% of success is the people chosen. A bad hire on a customer's property costs callbacks, theft risk, and crew culture — far more than three weeks of overtime. Trial weeks become permanent by drift.
principle_voice_en: Most of the unemployed are the people nobody else wanted.

scenario_en: You need a second foreman. Candidate one is the best installer you've ever tested — fast, clean, knows every product — but during the working interview he padded his hours by ninety minutes and bad-mouthed his last boss twice. Candidate two is slower, needs training on your pump systems, but his references say "honest to a fault" and he stayed seven years at one company.
option_a_en: Take candidate two and budget the training time — you can teach pumps, you can't teach honest.
option_b_en: Take candidate one and put controls around him — talent like that is rare.
option_c_en: Take candidate one as an installer only, where the timesheet padding matters less.
why_en: A foreman collects checks on driveways, signs change orders, and runs jobs unwatched. Skill gaps close with training; a character gap already showed you what he does when he thinks nobody's counting.
principle_voice_en: Trust distills to character and competence — and you can train competence.

scenario_en: After three interviews and a ride-along, your finalist for crew lead is... fine. Checks every box on paper, references are politely positive, but nobody on the crew is excited, and you keep talking yourself into him. Spring rush starts in five weeks and restarting the search means another month of you covering the slot personally.
option_a_en: Extend the offer — "fine" plus training usually becomes good, and the calendar is real.
option_b_en: Pass, restart the search, and keep covering the slot until a candidate makes you say "hell yeah."
option_c_en: Offer him a 90-day temp-to-perm deal so you're not fully committed.
why_en: If you don't love the candidate, don't hire — lukewarm hires become the mediocre middle you can't fire and can't promote. The pain of covering a slot is temporary; a wrong lead poisons a whole crew.
principle_voice_en: A team of level-7 talents who want to be here beats level-10 talents who aren't sure.

scenario_en: Marcus is your most precise installer — flawless work, lives for tolerances — but he's awkward with homeowners and hates running point. The open foreman job pays him $6/hour more, and he's next in line by seniority. Meanwhile your QC/punch-list backlog is killing you, and that role barely exists. Marcus asks about the foreman job.
option_a_en: Promote him — seniority matters, and he'll grow into the customer side.
option_b_en: Keep him installing and give the foreman job to the next guy down.
option_c_en: Build a paid QC/final-inspection role around his precision, with a raise, and tell him why he's perfect for it.
why_en: Put people where their strengths are valued and their weaknesses don't matter. Promoting a precision craftsman into a people job loses a great installer and gains a bad foreman.
principle_voice_en: Put people where their strengths are valued and their weaknesses don't matter.

scenario_en: Danny, eight months in, still can't set a discharge line to grade — his third callback for the same issue this quarter. He's likable, shows up early, and the crew covers for him. You've "mentioned it" twice but never actually trained the skill step-by-step. Letting it ride is easiest; the crew quietly redoes his lines anyway.
option_a_en: Move him to demo and hauling, where grading doesn't come up.
option_b_en: Keep letting the crew backstop him — it's working, and he's good for morale.
option_c_en: Run a real two-week training plan with checkpoints; if the skill doesn't land, move him out.
why_en: Hope is not a strategy, and "mentioning it" is not training. Train deliberately with a deadline; if it doesn't take, remove him before callbacks become your reputation.
principle_voice_en: What if I don't train them and they stay?

scenario_en: You're the production manager, and you're also the best installer in the company. Every time a job gets tricky you grab your tools — and this month, while you were under three houses, two crews sat waiting on material orders you didn't place and a permit you didn't pull. The owner asks why production fell 20% while you worked harder than ever.
option_a_en: Admit you've been doing the wrong job: stay out of the crawl spaces, run scheduling, materials, permits, and training.
option_b_en: Keep tooling up on the hardest jobs but come in Saturdays to catch up the paperwork.
option_c_en: Split it: tools in the morning, manager work after 2 p.m.
why_en: You're paid for the team's output, not your own hands. Every hour under a house cost two crews their materials and permits. The best installer in the company was the most expensive helper on it.
principle_voice_en: Doing everything yourself is a recipe for failure, frustration, burnout, and letting customers down.

scenario_en: You hand the tool-and-material inventory to your yard man: "Make it accurate." Three weeks later, two crews show up to jobs missing parts twice in one week. You're furious and tempted to just take inventory back — it was never wrong when you did it. He never got the count sheets, the reorder points, or a single check-in from you.
option_a_en: Take it back — some jobs are just yours.
option_b_en: Re-delegate properly: define "ready-to-roll trucks," give him count sheets and reorder points, weekly check-in, and tell him you believe he'll own it.
option_c_en: Keep him on it but quietly recount everything yourself each Friday night.
why_en: You didn't delegate — you abdicated. Clear result, resources, belief, and a check-in rhythm is delegation. Taking it back teaches everyone that handoffs from you are fake.
principle_voice_en: Tell them the result you expect and let them figure out how.

scenario_en: Your new foreman, two weeks in, left a job site at 3:30 with the driveway unswept and no customer walk-through. You're about to write him up. Then you check his onboarding: nobody ever walked him through your close-out standard — he came from a company where the office did all customer contact and crews just left.
option_a_en: Train the close-out standard today, have him run it on his next three jobs with you watching, then hold him to it.
option_b_en: Write him up — foremen should know jobsite basics anywhere.
option_c_en: Skip the write-up but mention at the crew meeting that close-outs have been slipping.
why_en: Expectation gaps cause execution gaps. You can't hold a man accountable to a standard that exists only in your head. Set it, train it, then accountability has teeth.
principle_voice_en: Expectation gaps lead to execution gaps. There is not a close second.

scenario_en: Luis has run your second crew for three years: zero callbacks this year, trains every new helper, never complains. He's never once been mentioned at a company meeting — the praise always goes to the big-revenue crew. Today the owner gives you five minutes in the all-hands and $500 of discretionary budget for "whatever production needs."
option_a_en: Put the $500 toward the impact driver the crews keep requesting — tools beat speeches.
option_b_en: Mention all crews equally so nobody feels left out.
option_c_en: Spend your five minutes on Luis — zero callbacks, by name, specifics — and give him the $500 as a quality award.
why_en: Recognition beats money, and the quiet day-in-day-outers are exactly who gets forgotten. Public, specific, genuine praise for Luis tells every foreman what gets celebrated here.
principle_voice_en: Pretend every employee has a sign around their neck that says, 'Make me feel important.

principle_title_en: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool
scenario_en: Your best installer has been off all week — late twice, quiet, a measuring mistake that's not like him. Friday you learn his wife was just laid off and their car died; he's been biking 40 minutes to the yard. You have a loaner shop truck nobody's using and a busy Saturday he'd normally want for overtime.
option_a_en: Give him space — good men work out their own problems, and he hasn't asked.
option_b_en: Lend him the shop truck for the month, give him Saturday's overtime, and ask what else would help.
option_c_en: Quietly assign him the easiest jobs until things settle down.
why_en: Help someone with their work and they like you; help them with their life and they love you. A truck and a Saturday cost you almost nothing and buy loyalty money can't.
principle_voice_en: Help someone with their work, and they like you. Help them with their life, and they love you.

principle_title_en: Give Away the Credit, Take the Blame
scenario_en: The owner walks a finished $38,000 job with the thrilled homeowner, then turns to you in front of your crew: "Beautiful work — this is why I made you production manager." Truth is, your foreman redesigned the drainage route mid-job and saved it after YOUR original layout hit ledge rock. The crew is watching you take the handshake.
option_a_en: Right there: "Thank Dave — my layout hit rock and his redesign saved this job. He's the reason it's beautiful."
option_b_en: Accept it graciously now, praise Dave at the next crew meeting.
option_c_en: Accept it — you built the team that built the job, and that's what managers get paid for.
why_en: Give away the credit in the moment it's offered, in front of the people who earned it. Wait a week and it's your story; do it now and every man digs harder for you.
principle_voice_en: GIVE AWAY THE CREDIT. TAKE THE BLAME.

principle_title_en: Never Act on One Side of a Story
scenario_en: A homeowner calls you, the production manager, furious: your foreman "stormed off the job at 1 p.m. and left a mess." She wants him banned from her property and a discount. The foreman is your steadiest guy in six years. Your gut says make it right with her immediately — she's threatening a one-star review tonight.
option_a_en: Tell her you take it seriously, you'll get the facts today, and call her back by 5 — then hear the foreman out.
option_b_en: Apologize, promise a different crew and a discount, then ask the foreman what happened.
option_c_en: Pull the foreman off and write him up tonight — protect the review first, sort facts later.
why_en: One sure way to take the wrong action is acting on half the story. Maybe he left because her dog bit a helper, or a gas smell. Commit to speed, not to a verdict.
principle_voice_en: One sure way to take the wrong action is to act on incomplete or incorrect information.

scenario_en: Final cleanup on a basement job, you notice a damp shadow at one corner seam — barely visible, probably condensation, maybe a weep. The customer hasn't seen it. Testing it means pulling a section of new wall panel and staying two hours late on a Friday. Odds are it's nothing, and the warranty covers it anyway if it ever shows up.
option_a_en: Note it in the file so service has a record if she ever calls.
option_b_en: Snap a photo and tell the customer to keep an eye on that corner.
option_c_en: Pull the panel and test it now, two hours late, while the tools are out and the fix is small.
why_en: Crisis causes are planted early. A weep found today is a two-hour fix; found in eight months it's a flooded carpet, a furious review, and a full crew callback.
principle_voice_en: Good leaders recognize when a fuse is lit and act right away.

principle_title_en: Culture Is When the Boss Leaves
scenario_en: You're back from two days at a trade show. Your helper mentions, casually, that while you were gone the crew skipped trench shoring on a four-foot dig "because the soil was solid" and finished early. Nobody got hurt; the job passed; the foreman who allowed it is your senior guy and the customer loved the speed.
option_a_en: Let it go with a quiet word to the foreman — no harm done, and you don't want to punish initiative.
option_b_en: Address it head-on: with the foreman privately, then re-set the shoring standard with all crews — what happens when you're gone IS the company.
option_c_en: Start doing surprise site visits so they never know when you're watching.
why_en: Culture is what happens when the boss leaves the building. A skipped safety standard that "worked" becomes the real standard. Surveillance can't fix culture; standards held without you can.
principle_voice_en: Culture is what happens when the boss leaves the building.

scenario_en: Mid-pour, your newest apprentice — three weeks in — says in front of the crew, "Isn't that footing form an inch out of square?" You check. He's wrong; it's within tolerance. Two veterans smirk. The crew is watching how you respond to the new kid who just questioned the foreman publicly.
option_a_en: Quietly tell him afterward to bring concerns to you privately, not in front of the crew.
option_b_en: Joke it off — "stick to mixing, rook" — and keep the pour moving.
option_c_en: Thank him loudly, show him the tolerance check, and tell the crew you want every set of eyes doing exactly that.
why_en: Each time someone speaks up is a test. Punish a wrong catch and you lose every future right one — the next bad footing gets poured in silence while the crew watches.
principle_voice_en: Each time someone speaks up is a test — never embarrass anyone, and use the best ideas no matter where they come from.

scenario_en: Your crew opens a job and finds the salesperson under-measured the wall run by 30 feet — third time this quarter with the same rep. The crew wants you to call the customer and tell her "sales messed up, this will cost more." It would feel great, and it's even true. The change order needs to happen either way.
option_a_en: Handle the change order as "the company" — no blame to the customer — then fix the measuring problem directly with sales the same week.
option_b_en: Tell the customer plainly that the estimate was sales' error so production doesn't eat the blame.
option_c_en: Absorb the 30 feet quietly this time and send sales an email about it.
why_en: To the customer there is one company, win or lose together. Throwing sales under the bus buys your crew nothing and costs the company trust. Fix it internally, where it can actually get fixed.
principle_voice_en: We all win or lose together — the company is one department.

principle_title_en: Serve the Human, Not the House
scenario_en: Day one at Mrs. Alvarez's house: 81, recently widowed, hovering nervously as your crew jackhammers her basement floor. She asks the same questions three times and apologizes for it. Your crew is on a foreman-bonus pace and every minute talking is a minute not digging. Your helper mutters, "Just work around her."
option_a_en: Be polite but keep the crew heads-down — the best gift you can give her is a finished basement.
option_b_en: Assign her a person: you check in each morning, lunch, and day's end, walk her through what's next, write your cell on the contract.
option_c_en: Suggest she stay upstairs for safety until the loud work is done.
why_en: You're not servicing a house, you're servicing a human being — a scared one. Ten scheduled minutes of communication a day costs less than one panicked mid-job cancellation or a worried daughter's phone call.
principle_voice_en: We are not servicing a house, we are servicing a human being.

scenario_en: Job's done a half-day early and under budget — contract delivered, customer satisfied. You have the crew until 3:00. The customer's sagging gate caught your eye all week; a fix is twenty minutes and scrap lumber. Your helper says, "Satisfied is the goal, boss, let's load up." Dispatch would happily take you back early.
option_a_en: Head in early — finishing early IS the wow, and dispatch can use you.
option_b_en: Fix the gate, mention it at the walk-through, and ask who else she knows who needs us.
option_c_en: Fix the gate, mention it at the walk-through, ask for referrals AND a review while the crew's still there.
why_en: Satisfied customers tell no one. The twenty-minute gate plus telling her about it plus asking on the spot is the whole flywheel — Wow produces referrals only if you say it and ask.
principle_voice_en: The standard is not 'no complaints' but a customer who says 'Wow!

principle_title_en: The Experience Is Half the Product
scenario_en: Your waterproofing work is the best in the county — and your truck is a rolling junk drawer. This morning's customer watched your crew track mud across her hall, crank a country station, and dig lunch wrappers off the dash for the contract copy. The install underneath will be perfect. Your foreman shrugs: "We're judged on the system, not the seat covers."
option_a_en: He's right — invest your energy in the install quality; the warranty speaks for itself.
option_b_en: Re-set the standard today: floor protection, clean truck, music off, shoe covers — the customer can't see the install; she judges what she CAN see.
option_c_en: Have the office call her with a quality-survey afterward to balance the impression.
why_en: Customers can't judge a drainage system; they infer the quality of what they can't see from the quality of what they can. Mud in the hallway IS the product to her.
principle_voice_en: Anyone can do the work, but not anyone provides a great Customer Experience.

scenario_en: Monday 7:40 a.m., a customer from last month calls you directly: her new sump pump ran all night and there's water on the floor again. She's near tears — she has family visiting Thursday. Your week is fully booked, every crew committed, and the service tech is out sick. Technically her callback could slot next Monday.
option_a_en: Tell her you'll personally be there by noon today, pull yourself off planning, and call her back at 11 with your ETA.
option_b_en: Book her first slot next Monday and waive the service fee for the trouble.
option_c_en: Slot her Thursday morning — before the family arrives, without breaking this week's schedule.
why_en: Handle a complaint fast and right, and the customer ends up happier than if nothing went wrong. Speed is the apology. A week of efficient scheduling isn't worth one drowned referral source.
principle_voice_en: Problems are opportunities — act fast and take responsibility.

scenario_en: Production is slammed, and on the board sits a day of annual maintenance visits — past customers, $190 each, booked under the service plan you sold them at install. Your biggest new job is behind, and pulling that tech for a day catches it up. Maintenance customers "never notice" a few weeks' slip, the scheduler says.
option_a_en: Slip the maintenance visits three weeks — new installs pay the bills.
option_b_en: Run the maintenance day as scheduled — those past customers are your cheapest future jobs, referrals, and reviews.
option_c_en: Compromise: do the maintenance by phone check-in now, visit when things calm down.
why_en: You either let customers go after the job or keep them forever — and the annual visit is how "forever" happens. Past customers are gold: they buy again, refer, and cost nothing to win.
principle_voice_en: Keep customers for life by staying in their mind for life.

scenario_en: Wrapping a crawl-space job, your installer shows you the customer's water heater: corroded fittings, rust streak, clearly on borrowed time. Your company replaces them. You're not on commission for the visit and mentioning it feels like "being a salesman." If it bursts in that crawl space, everything you just encapsulated gets soaked.
option_a_en: Note it on the close-out paperwork and let the office decide whether to call.
option_b_en: Stay in your lane — homeowners hate upsells from the crew.
option_c_en: Show the homeowner the corrosion now, explain what failure looks like, and offer to have your company quote the replacement.
why_en: Fail to sell and they keep their problem — and yours floods. A foreman has more credibility than any salesperson; you're not pitching, you're warning someone about a failure you can see.
principle_voice_en: The tech or foreman in the home has MORE credibility than the salesperson.

scenario_en: During a $4,000 crack repair at a small, tired-looking ranch house — older cars, worn furniture — the homeowner asks your foreman what a full perimeter system "would even run." The real answer involves a design visit and likely $30,000+. Your foreman tells you later he changed the subject: "No way she can swing that. Didn't want to embarrass her."
option_a_en: Coach him today: never pre-judge a wallet — offer everyone the design visit and let HER decide; book it on your follow-up call.
option_b_en: Back his read — pushing a $30,000 conversation on a fixed income borders on predatory.
option_c_en: Have the office mail her a brochure about the full system so the door stays open.
why_en: Pre-qualifying causes the no. Worn furniture says nothing about savings, insurance money, or what a dry basement is worth to her. Deciding for the customer robs her of the choice.
principle_voice_en: Never pre-judge or pre-qualify an appointment.

scenario_en: Mid-install, the homeowner sidles up to you with coffee: "While you guys are here — ballpark, what would it cost to do the other wall too?" You've roughed jobs like it a hundred times; the number in your head is around $8,500. He's friendly, he's standing right there, and "I can't say" feels evasive and salesy.
option_a_en: Give a soft range — "probably eight to ten" — and tell him sales will firm it up.
option_b_en: Tell him that wall deserves real measurements and a real design — and offer to get the design specialist out this week, maybe even today.
option_c_en: Deflect with "I just build 'em" and leave a salesperson's card on the counter.
why_en: No ballpark estimates, ever, by anyone. Your "eight-to-ten" becomes the ceiling sales must sell under, with zero value built. The honest answer is a process, not a number.
principle_voice_en: Never reveal a price before a full presentation builds value.

scenario_en: At close-out, the customer says, "We'll do the egress window and the dehumidifier next year, once we catch our breath." That's $11,000 of designed, quoted, customer-approved work — just not yet. Your close-out sheet has no field for it, the salesperson has moved on to new leads, and in your experience "next year" usually evaporates.
option_a_en: Leave it with the customer — she knows the number and where to find you.
option_b_en: Tell the salesperson at the next meeting so it's back on his radar.
option_c_en: Log it as an unsold-work record with a date, confirm with her "we'll check in this fall," and make sure the office Hunter list gets it.
why_en: Every company leaves more work unsold than sold — that's the gold. Follow-up happens through systems, not memories. "Until the sale is made" starts with writing it down before you leave.
principle_voice_en: I WILL KEEP FOLLOWING UP – FOREVER, UNTIL THE SALE IS MADE.

scenario_en: Final walk-through done, customer thrilled, crew loading the truck. The $7,400 final payment is due on completion — it's in the contract. The customer waves you off warmly: "I'll drop a check in the mail this week, I promise. My checkbook's at my office." You have another job starting in an hour and pushing feels awkward after such a good week.
option_a_en: Stay friendly and stay put: offer card, bank app, or a ride to her office — payment on completion is the agreement, collect before you leave.
option_b_en: Take her word — she's a great customer, and trust is part of the relationship.
option_c_en: Accept mailing it but have her sign a promissory note for the balance.
why_en: Collect before you leave — otherwise you haven't done your job. The day you drive away, your leverage and her urgency leave with you. Receivables are where cash goes to die.
principle_voice_en: Cash is life. If you run out of cash, you are out of business!

scenario_en: The owner asks you, the production manager, why gross margin on installs dropped four points this quarter. You honestly can't say — you don't job-cost. Crews feel busy, jobs finish "around" schedule, and material runs to the supply house happen whenever. You could pull labor hours and material invoices job-by-job for a sample, but it's tedious and you're slammed.
option_a_en: Tell the owner margins move around seasonally and you'll watch it next quarter.
option_b_en: Job-cost a sample now — a small, medium, and large job per service — and find exactly where hours and materials are leaking.
option_c_en: Tighten everything at once: freeze overtime and require approval on all material runs.
why_en: Running production without job costs is stepping on the gas with your eyes closed. A strategic sample shows which jobs lose money and why — then you fix causes, not guess at them.
principle_voice_en: Being busy growing the company and not watching the numbers is like stepping on the gas and closing your eyes.

principle_title_en: Pay for What You Want Repeated
scenario_en: Your installers are hourly, and jobs mysteriously fill whatever time the schedule allows — a two-day job takes two days or three, depending on nothing you can name. The owner offers to let you redesign crew pay. A by-the-job rate would speed crews up, but you worry they'll rush quality to bank hours. Callbacks would land on next quarter's books.
option_a_en: Stay hourly but add a speed bonus for finishing early.
option_b_en: Pay by the job — with the rate docked for any callback or failed inspection on that job, so speed and quality pay the same man.
option_c_en: Pay by the job, straight — trust the crews' pride to protect quality.
why_en: Pay by the hour, get hours. Pay by the job, get speed — and get gaming unless quality is wired into the same incentive. Design the metric so the shortcut doesn't pay.
principle_voice_en: Pay foremen by the job, not the hour — people who make good money value their jobs and look out for the company.

scenario_en: Tony, your senior foreman, is a legend — carries every job sequence, supplier contact, and inspection quirk in his head. Nothing is written down. He just asked for two weeks off in July, and you realized his crew can't function a day without him. He's also 58, and a competitor has been sniffing around him for months.
option_a_en: Spend the next 60 days turning Tony's head into checklists, job-start scripts, and a daily-discipline routine — paying him extra to build and teach it.
option_b_en: Give Tony a raise and a retention bonus — keep the genius happy and in the building.
option_c_en: Deny long vacations during season — that's the cost of being indispensable.
why_en: Predictability equals scalability. A hero in the gear isn't a system — he's a single point of failure with a retirement date. Paying him to systematize himself honors him AND protects you.
principle_voice_en: Predictability = Scalability.

principle_title_en: How We Do Anything Is How We Do Everything
scenario_en: End of a long Thursday: a $300 warranty touch-up at a tiny job for a customer who never leaves reviews. Your crew wants to skip the floor tarps, the photos, and the close-out walk-through "just this once — it's a twenty-minute caulk job, boss." The full routine adds maybe twenty-five minutes. Nobody from the office will ever check.
option_a_en: Skip the extras — judgment means matching effort to stakes, and the stakes are $300.
option_b_en: Do tarps and the walk-through, skip the photos — reasonable middle ground.
option_c_en: Run the full standard — tarps, photos, walk-through, referral ask. There is no job small enough to do our way halfway.
why_en: How we do anything is how we do everything. Crews that learn standards have exceptions will find exceptions everywhere. The $300 job is where your real culture gets rehearsed for the $50,000 one.
principle_voice_en: EVERYTHING COUNTS.

scenario_en: You're the office manager. The owner says the financials "never feel trustworthy." You look: miscoded entries, a bloated Misc account, reconciliations weeks behind. Nobody else touches QuickBooks — these books are yours. The owner asks what's going on.
option_a_en: Explain that QuickBooks is the problem and request new software.
option_b_en: Own it: the books mirror your habits. Set coding rules, empty Misc, reconcile weekly, raise your personal standard.
option_c_en: Quietly fix this month's entries and hope the question goes away.
why_en: The books are the keeper's elongated shadow. They will not get better until you do. Blaming tools or patching one month leaves the source — your standards — untouched.
principle_voice_en: The business is the leader's elongated shadow — it will not get better until he does.

scenario_en: Receivables have crept from 20 days to 60. You've been telling yourself it's the salespeople's vague payment terms and slow-paying customers. The owner pulls the aging report and asks you, the bookkeeper, what happened.
option_a_en: Say "I own this number" — then build a collection routine: invoice same-day, call at 25 days, track it weekly.
option_b_en: Send the owner a memo documenting how sales caused it.
option_c_en: Explain the economy is slow right now; it should self-correct.
why_en: Total responsibility is the starting line. Ask "How did I cause this?" The aging report is your scoreboard; once you own it, you can change it.
principle_voice_en: Whatever your organization is today, ask 'How did I cause this?

scenario_en: Reconciling the bank, you discover you paid a supplier invoice twice — $4,200, three months ago. The owner already saw the bank statement and knows it was your miss. You feel sick about it.
option_a_en: Apologize hard and avoid touching payables decisions for a while.
option_b_en: Recover the money quietly and never bring it up again.
option_c_en: Recover the $4,200, then build a duplicate-payment check into your close so this error can never repeat.
why_en: Setbacks are poison or fuel — you choose. Failing, learning fast, and never repeating the grade turns a $4,200 mistake into a permanent system upgrade.
principle_voice_en: Mistakes are the world giving you feedback — nothing personal. Never repeat a grade in the School of Hard Knocks.

scenario_en: The owner offers to pay for SOE financial classes — Your Spread, Job Cost Sampling, Calculating Labor Burden. You've done the books the same way for nine years and month-end always runs tight. It feels like there's no time.
option_a_en: Decline politely — close week leaves no room for classes.
option_b_en: Skim the class summaries during lunch and call it done.
option_c_en: Take the classes and apply one new lesson to every monthly close until it's habit.
why_en: Nine years of the same year isn't nine years of experience. Knowledge plus experience plus reflection compounds; a learning machine gets more valuable every close.
principle_voice_en: Wisdom = Knowledge + Experience + Reflection.

scenario_en: It's the 12th. Statements are due to the owner on the 15th — every month, no exceptions. Two supplier invoices haven't arrived, maybe $3,000 of job costs. You could hold the close and deliver "perfect" numbers around the 25th.
option_a_en: Accrue your best estimate for the missing invoices, close on time, true it up next month.
option_b_en: Wait for the real invoices — accuracy matters more than a deadline.
option_c_en: Skip this month and roll it into a clean quarterly statement.
why_en: Statements by the 15th, every month, no exceptions — that's the basic. A small, honest accrual keeps the rhythm; a "perfect" late statement breaks the discipline that makes numbers useful.
principle_voice_en: Doing simple things consistently makes all the difference — easy to do, easy not to do.

scenario_en: Cash-basis QuickBooks shows a $38,000 profit, but the checking account is nearly empty — customer deposits came in, the work isn't done, and big bills are unpaid. The owner is thrilled with "the best month ever" and wants to celebrate.
option_a_en: Leave the report as-is — he's happy, and the view is technically a setting.
option_b_en: Convert to accrual: deposits are a liability, revenue is work completed and billed. Show him the real month.
option_c_en: Tell him it's just a timing issue that will wash out by year end.
why_en: The first job of a leader is to define reality. Cash basis flatters; accrual tells the truth. Deposits are work you OWE, not money you earned.
principle_voice_en: Fake News. If you want to show a bigger profit on cash basis accounting, just don't pay your bills.

scenario_en: The owner walks in: "I found a great deal on a service truck — $48,000. Cut the check today before it's gone." There's no truck in this year's budget, and you haven't modeled what the payment does to cash.
option_a_en: Cut the check — it's his company and his call.
option_b_en: Suggest leasing instead so the hit feels smaller.
option_c_en: Ask for 24 hours: build the truck into the cash model and budget, show the effect on the Spread, then decide.
why_en: Everything is created twice — first on paper, then in reality. A purchase modeled first is a decision; a purchase rushed is a gamble with payroll money.
principle_voice_en: Use your models — Business Machine, Dream Machine, Cash Calculator — to see where the company is going.

scenario_en: You closed on time. But gross margin dropped six points this month, and you don't know why. The owner's review meeting is tomorrow morning. You could present the statements as-is — the close is technically done.
option_a_en: Dig in tonight: job-cost the month, isolate which jobs and which cost lines moved, and bring the cause.
option_b_en: Present the statements and note "margin dipped — probably material prices."
option_c_en: Reclassify a few direct costs to overhead so margin looks normal.
why_en: Closing the books isn't the job — explaining them is. Numbers are effects; your value is naming the cause behind every number, not just confirming it balanced.
principle_voice_en: Numbers are the effects of other things going on in the company — find the activities that cause them to change.

scenario_en: Your owner takes random draws whenever the account looks fat, and no salary. The P&L shows a proud "profit" — but nobody has been paid to run the company. He asks why you want to "complicate things" with an owner salary.
option_a_en: Leave it — draws keep things simple and flexible.
option_b_en: Set a fair manager's salary for the job he actually does, so the profit line is real profit AFTER his pay.
option_c_en: Suggest he skip pay in slow months so the statements always look profitable.
why_en: The business serves its owner — it pays him like it pays everyone else. Profit is what remains AFTER a market salary. Anything else is a pretty number hiding an unpaid job.
principle_voice_en: Take a manager's salary for the job you do — profit is what remains AFTER you're paid like everyone else.

principle_title_en: Do Right When It Costs You
scenario_en: Brutal month: a warranty job ate margin and a big receivable went sideways. The statement is due the 15th — Friday — the same day the owner leaves for his first vacation in two years. Holding it a week would be easy and kind.
option_a_en: Hold the statement until he's back, rested and ready.
option_b_en: Soften it — push some costs into next month so the trend looks gentler.
option_c_en: Deliver it accurate and on time, with a clear written "why" for each ugly number and your plan.
why_en: Accurate and on time, especially when it hurts — that's the whole job. He already feels the truth; an honest statement with causes and a plan respects him and protects trust.
principle_voice_en: Be honest about where the company is — they already know, and honesty buys credibility for the rest.

principle_title_en: Hiring Makes You or Breaks You
scenario_en: Your AP clerk quit and bills are piling up. One candidate can start Monday — decent interview, but you haven't checked references or run a background check, and she'd touch every vendor payment. The owner says "your call."
option_a_en: Slow down one week: background check, reference calls, and a skills test before anyone touches payables.
option_b_en: Hire her Monday — the backlog is the bigger risk right now.
option_c_en: Don't hire; absorb AP into your own job permanently.
why_en: A money-handling hire makes you or breaks you. A week of vetting is cheap; a bad hire in payables can cost years. Hire slow, especially near the checkbook.
principle_voice_en: Know your people before and after hiring — past criminals are far more likely to offend again.

scenario_en: Two bookkeeper finalists. One is a QuickBooks wizard with five years of job-cost experience — but a reference hints she "borrowed" petty cash at her last job. The other is honest, organized, and teachable, but you'd have to train her up.
option_a_en: Hire the wizard but watch her closely with extra oversight.
option_b_en: Hire the honest, teachable one and invest in training her skills.
option_c_en: Hire the wizard and keep the reference comment to yourself — it's hearsay.
why_en: Skill can be taught; character can't. A skilled keeper with a theft whisper in her past is a loaded risk sitting next to your bank account. Surveillance is not a substitute for integrity.
principle_voice_en: Trust distills to character and competence.

scenario_en: Mid-close, a software vendor calls pitching an analytics add-on: dashboards, AI categorization, a free trial. It's mildly interesting. Saying yes means demos, data migration, emails, and training time — all during your busiest two weeks.
option_a_en: Buy the trial — it might help and it's free to start.
option_b_en: Schedule three demo calls to be polite and "stay informed."
option_c_en: Say no — short, polite, final — and protect the close. Revisit only if it becomes a clear "hell yeah."
why_en: Every yes steals time from what you already said yes to. A lukewarm "maybe" during close week costs the company its most important deadline. Mild interest is a no.
principle_voice_en: Better a few seconds of regret from saying no than months of regret from saying yes.

scenario_en: Your AR clerk is warm and great on the phone but hates detail — her reconciliations keep slipping. Your other office employee is a quiet Thinker who loves spreadsheets and dreads collection calls. Both are struggling in their current seats.
option_a_en: Swap the work: the people-person takes collection calls, the Thinker takes reconciliations.
option_b_en: Send both to a training class on their weak areas.
option_c_en: Write up the AR clerk for the missed reconciliations.
why_en: Don't train against nature when you can re-seat with it. Put people where strengths are valued and weaknesses don't matter — two struggling employees become two strong ones overnight.
principle_voice_en: Put people where their strengths are valued and their weaknesses don't matter.

scenario_en: Foremen turn in job sheets with missing hours and no material counts, so your job-cost reports are garbage. You've sent two reminder emails. Nobody has ever actually taught the foremen what job costing is or why it matters.
option_a_en: Stop job costing — the data's too messy to be worth it.
option_b_en: Run a short training: show foremen how a job sheet becomes a job cost, role-play it, then hold the standard.
option_c_en: Have the office estimate the missing hours and keep going.
why_en: Untrained people are good people not led well. Emails aren't training. Teach the why and the how, make them do it, then expect it — or you'll guess at margins forever.
principle_voice_en: What if I don't train them and they stay?

scenario_en: You're the controller. Your statements are immaculate and always on time. The Spread has fallen two months straight and the aging is creeping — but nobody's said anything, and you figure the owner reads the reports. The monthly meeting is today.
option_a_en: Stay quiet — your job is producing accurate reports, and you did.
option_b_en: Email the spreadsheet to the owner afterward with the trend highlighted.
option_c_en: Raise it in the meeting, out loud: "Spread is down two months running — here's why, and here's what I recommend."
why_en: You're the Defensive Coordinator, not a quiet numbers assembler. Defense calls plays out loud. An unspoken warning protects no one; the watchdog's job is to bark early.
principle_voice_en: Watch the windshield, not just the mirror.

scenario_en: The owner, swamped with sales, says: "Take it all — checks, signing, bank statements, everything. Don't bother me with money stuff anymore." It's flattering. You'd have total control of the company's cash with zero oversight.
option_a_en: Push back: you'll run daily finance, but he keeps signing checks and gets bank statements at home, unopened by anyone.
option_b_en: Accept it all — this is what real trust looks like.
option_c_en: Accept it all but promise him a quarterly summary.
why_en: Owners deputize finance; they never surrender it. Total control with no oversight endangers the company and YOU — when something goes missing, the unwatched bookkeeper is suspect number one.
principle_voice_en: You can hire someone to do your accounting, but you can't hire someone to understand the numbers and make decisions.

scenario_en: The new foreman has left three jobs without collecting final payment, and you're chasing customers by phone for thousands. You're furious — then you realize nobody ever told him the payment terms or that collecting before leaving is his job.
option_a_en: Report him to the owner as careless with company money.
option_b_en: Keep chasing the payments yourself — it's faster than a confrontation.
option_c_en: Set the expectation first: written payment terms, "collect before you leave" in the job checklist, then hold him to it.
why_en: You can't hold people accountable to expectations they never received. Define the standard clearly, equip him, then accountability is fair — and the receivables problem dies at the source.
principle_voice_en: In the absence of leadership, people copy other employees or invent survival strategies.

scenario_en: Your quiet AR clerk just pulled the aging under 30 days for the first time in company history and caught a $1,100 duplicate billing before it went out. She never asks for attention. You're busy, and praise feels awkward.
option_a_en: Save it for her annual review where it "counts."
option_b_en: Praise her now, by name, in front of the team — specific numbers, sincere words.
option_c_en: Say nothing — collections and accuracy are literally her job.
why_en: People will do more for recognition than for money — especially the quiet day-in-day-outers. Praise the collections win and the caught leak publicly, and you'll see both repeated.
principle_voice_en: Remember the quiet day-in-day-outers, not just stars.

principle_title_en: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool
scenario_en: Your payroll clerk — five years, rock solid — has made three errors in two weeks, including a wrong direct deposit. Then you learn her mother just entered hospice. Payroll runs Friday, and accuracy genuinely matters.
option_a_en: Sit with her, ask about her mom, shift work off her plate, and add a second-check step so payroll stays safe.
option_b_en: Issue a written warning — payroll errors are serious regardless of circumstances.
option_c_en: Quietly redo her work yourself and say nothing to her.
why_en: Care for the person AND protect the payroll — they're not in conflict. Help her with her life, not just her work, and you earn loyalty no salary can buy.
principle_voice_en: Help someone with their work, and they like you. Help them with their life, and they love you.

principle_title_en: Give Away the Credit, Take the Blame
scenario_en: A lien deadline was missed on a $19,000 unpaid job — your office's miss, though your AP clerk had the calendar. Separately, your team's new deposit process just cut posting errors in half. The owner asks about both at the staff meeting.
option_a_en: Take the lien miss yourself — "my system failed" — and credit the clerk's team by name for the deposit win.
option_b_en: Be accurate: name the clerk on the miss, take credit for the process you designed.
option_c_en: Mention only the deposit win and handle the lien quietly later.
why_en: Leaders who absorb blame and give away credit get people fixing problems instead of hiding them. "Accuracy" about fault buys nothing; ownership buys a team that protects deadlines.
principle_voice_en: GIVE AWAY THE CREDIT. TAKE THE BLAME.

principle_title_en: Never Act on One Side of a Story
scenario_en: Job-cost review shows the Hendricks job at 64 labor hours against 40 estimated. The salesman storms in: "Your foreman padded his hours — dock him." The numbers do look bad. The foreman is on a jobsite an hour away.
option_a_en: The data is the data — flag the foreman's timesheet as suspect in the file.
option_b_en: Call the foreman first: walk the job hour by hour before any conclusion reaches anyone.
option_c_en: Split the difference in the job-cost report so nobody fights.
why_en: Never act on a one-sided report. Maybe he padded; maybe the estimate missed a crawlspace, or rain killed a day. The variance is a question, not a verdict — investigate, then act.
principle_voice_en: Never act on one-sided reports.

scenario_en: Mrs. Alvarez owes $6,800, now 32 days old. She's a sweet repeat customer, you're slammed with close week, and the owner never looks at anything under 60 days. One friendly call today — or let it ride to next month's aging.
option_a_en: Wait for 60 days, then send the standard past-due letter.
option_b_en: Let it ride — repeat customers always pay eventually.
option_c_en: Call today, warm and brief: confirm she got the invoice, confirm a pay date, note it in the file.
why_en: A receivable at 30 days is a phone call; at 120 it's a fight, a lien, or a loss. Red flags are cheapest the day they appear. Small now, or big later.
principle_voice_en: Investigate overdue receivables right away.

principle_title_en: Culture Is When the Boss Leaves
scenario_en: The owner is away for three weeks. Gas card spending jumps 30%, two crews started turning in cards' receipts late, and a tech asked you to "just push my hours through" without a signed timesheet. Everyone knows nobody's watching.
option_a_en: Document everything quietly and hand the owner a report when he returns.
option_b_en: Hold the standard exactly as if he were here: receipts required, signed timesheets required, and tell the team why.
option_c_en: Let small stuff slide for three weeks — morale matters and he'll be back soon.
why_en: Culture is what happens when the boss leaves — and fraud grows wherever nobody watches. Three weeks of slack teaches the whole company that controls are theater. The standard is the standard.
principle_voice_en: Every fraud story begins with 'I trusted them.

scenario_en: Your job-cost sampling shows the senior installer's jobs — the owner's favorite — consistently run 15% over on materials. Last year someone raised a cost issue about him and got frozen out for months. You publish the monthly trends.
option_a_en: Publish the trend but leave his jobs out of the sample this quarter.
option_b_en: Publish the real numbers for everyone, framed as "what the jobs are telling us" — facts, no blame, same rules for all.
option_c_en: Tell the owner privately and let him decide if it gets published.
why_en: Finance's job is truth in a form people can hear. Curated numbers teach everyone the reports are political. Publish real trends without punishing messengers — including when the messenger is the data.
principle_voice_en: Use the best ideas no matter where they come from — never embarrass anyone for speaking up.

scenario_en: A foreman calls from a driveway: the customer disputes a $900 change order and won't sign the final invoice. Your books say $900, clean and documented. The foreman needs an answer now; the customer is standing right there.
option_a_en: Tell him billing isn't decided in driveways — the customer can call the office Monday.
option_b_en: Hold firm on $900 and have the foreman leave the invoice unsigned.
