option_c_en: Take the call now, hear the customer, pull the change-order paperwork live, and solve it before the foreman leaves.
why_en: There's only one department: customer service. A billing dispute IS the customer experience, and accounting serves the field. Solve it while the tools are out — after you leave, it's a big deal.
principle_voice_en: Encourage customers to voice concerns while the tools are out — problems caught then are easy fixes.

principle_title_en: Serve the Human, Not the House
scenario_en: An elderly widow calls confused about her invoice — she thought the deposit covered more, and she sounds embarrassed and scared. You have six calls holding and the paperwork clearly supports the balance due. You're right; she's overwhelmed.
option_a_en: Slow down, use her name, walk the invoice line by line until she understands, and offer to mail a simple summary.
option_b_en: Email her the signed contract and deposit receipt — the documents speak for themselves.
option_c_en: Offer a discount so the call ends quickly.
why_en: A billing call is a human moment, not a paperwork transaction. She doesn't need to lose to documents or be bought off — she needs ten patient minutes. Serve the person, and the balance follows.
principle_voice_en: People will forget what you did — they never forget how you made them feel.

scenario_en: Your invoices are accurate but ugly: cramped codes, no job description, payment instructions buried. Customers call confused every week. Redesigning the QuickBooks template — plain-English line items, photo of completed work, clear due date, thank-you note — would take an afternoon.
option_a_en: Keep the standard template — accuracy is what an invoice is for.
option_b_en: Spend the afternoon: build an invoice so clear and professional a customer might actually say "Wow."
option_c_en: Add a "call us with questions" line to the current template.
why_en: Wow! is the standard for everything that touches a customer — including invoices. A clear, accurate, on-time invoice builds trust, cuts confused calls, and gets paid faster. Everything counts.
principle_voice_en: EVERYTHING COUNTS.

principle_title_en: The Experience Is Half the Product
scenario_en: Production says the Keller job is done. Standard practice: invoice mails in about a week, and if it goes unpaid, a form letter follows. You realize the invoice and any collection call are the customer's last two memories of the company.
option_a_en: Keep the routine — billing is back-office, not customer experience.
option_b_en: Email the invoice immediately with no other changes — speed is what counts.
option_c_en: Treat both as Moments of Truth: same-day invoice thanking them by name, and any follow-up call scripted warm and helpful.
why_en: The experience is half the product, and billing is the finale. The last touch is what they remember and repeat to neighbors. Design the invoice and the call like you'd design the jobsite.
principle_voice_en: The standard is not 'no complaints' but a customer who says 'Wow!

scenario_en: Monday morning: an angry voicemail. A customer was double-charged $2,400 when her financing payment AND her check both processed. She's threatening a bank dispute and a one-star review. It's posting day and your desk is buried.
option_a_en: Call her within the hour, apologize, refund today, and confirm in writing when it clears — then fix why it happened.
option_b_en: Verify everything carefully first and respond in two or three days with a complete answer.
option_c_en: Let the bank dispute process handle it — that's what the process is for.
why_en: A billing problem handled with speed and grace can win a customer more deeply than no problem at all. Tests are graded on response time. Refund first, root-cause second.
principle_voice_en: Complaints after you leave are a big deal.

scenario_en: The Romeros — $40,000 of work over eight years, three referrals — are 75 days late on a $2,200 service invoice for the first time ever. The standard process says: final demand letter, then collections agency. The letter is queued to print.
option_a_en: Send the demand letter — fair process means the same letter for everyone.
option_b_en: Call personally first: "This isn't like you — is everything okay?" Then work out a date or a plan.
option_c_en: Write off $2,200 as the cost of keeping a great relationship.
why_en: Graceful collections protect lifetime value. An eight-year customer earns a human call before a form letter. You'll usually find an illness or a lost invoice — and keep the next $40,000.
principle_voice_en: This customer chose your company; without them we are all out of a job.

scenario_en: A salesman closed a $14,000 foundation job contingent on financing, and the customer's application sits half-finished in the portal — confusing income fields, an upload that failed. The customer genuinely needs this repair. Administering financing is "not really" your job.
option_a_en: Email the customer the lender's help-line number.
option_b_en: Tell the salesman financing paperwork belongs to sales.
option_c_en: Call the customer, walk the application together screen by screen, and shepherd it to approval today.
why_en: Selling is helping, and financing administration is how the office helps a family afford work they need. The sale isn't done until the money works — and you're the one who speaks lender.
principle_voice_en: The customer wants the work done — your job is to help them decide.

scenario_en: Two snap judgments in one morning: a new customer from a rough zip code wants a payment plan ("they'll never pay," says your gut), and the Murphy job ran 20 hours over ("the foreman's padding," says the salesman). You've verified neither.
option_a_en: Run the same credit process for the customer as anyone, and walk the Murphy job with the foreman before concluding anything.
option_b_en: Require a bigger deposit from the customer and quietly audit the foreman's last five timesheets.
option_c_en: Trust your gut on both — pattern recognition is experience.
why_en: Never pre-judge — not the customer's wallet, not the foreman's honesty. Judgments without evidence cost you good customers and good people. Same process, same fairness, every time.
principle_voice_en: Never pre-judge or pre-qualify.

scenario_en: A property manager dangles ten crawlspace jobs for a 15% discount, and the owner wants your blessing today. Your last labor-burden calc is two years old, and you suspect net margin is thinner than the owner believes. 15% might be the whole profit.
option_a_en: Bless it — ten jobs of volume covers a lot of sins.
option_b_en: Run true costs first — fully loaded burden, real margin — then approve a discount only as big as the costs that actually drop.
option_c_en: Counter at 8% as a safe middle number.
why_en: Never price before you know value AND cost. Volume only earns a discount where it truly cuts cost — less marketing, no sales call, batched mobilization. Discounting blind is donating your net margin.
principle_voice_en: What you classify as direct cost determines your gross profit.

scenario_en: Mr. Tate owes $3,400, now 95 days. He's promised payment twice and gone quiet twice. Your last bookkeeper used to just write these off around 90 days "to keep the books clean." The lien window is still open for three more weeks.
option_a_en: Write it off — 95 days of silence is your answer.
option_b_en: Send one certified final-demand letter and stop calling.
option_c_en: Keep a polite cadence — call, letter, offer a payment plan — and protect the lien deadline now so you never lose the right.
why_en: Follow up forever, with grace. Persistence is professional, not rude — most silent debtors are embarrassed or strapped, not hostile. And never let a lien deadline lapse while you're being patient.
principle_voice_en: Most salespeople are poor at follow-up — there is real money in old leads.

scenario_en: Friday math: $61,000 cash, $48,000 receivables, $74,000 payables — the Spread just went negative for the first time. A supplier offers 2%/10 on a $20,000 invoice, payroll hits Friday, and two finished jobs are sitting unbilled from Tuesday.
option_a_en: Bill the finished jobs today, push collections hard toward zero receivables, take the 2%/10 discount, and report the Spread to the owner now.
option_b_en: Skip the discount and sit on all payables to hoard cash.
option_c_en: Spread looks scary but payroll clears — recheck the numbers at month end.
why_en: Cash is life and the Spread is your early-warning light. A dollar today beats a dollar next month: bill instantly, collect to zero, pay early (2%/10 is ~24% annual) — never late. And sound the alarm.
principle_voice_en: Cash is life. If you run out of cash, you are out of business!

scenario_en: At dinner, the owner's banker asks him: "What's your monthly break-even? Your fully loaded labor cost? Your net margin?" He couldn't answer any of them. Monday he asks you — and honestly, you'd be guessing too. The data exists; nobody's done the work.
option_a_en: Give him good-faith ballpark answers so he's never embarrassed again.
option_b_en: Build the real numbers: break even to the dollar, fully loaded labor burden, job-cost sampling, and net margin tracked as the #1 KPI.
option_c_en: Suggest the CPA can run those at tax time.
why_en: Know your numbers means KNOW — break even to the dollar, burden fully loaded, margins verified by job-cost sampling. Net margin is the #1 KPI. Guesses dressed as numbers are the most dangerous kind.
principle_voice_en: The numbers aren't hard — if you don't get it, you aren't trying.

principle_title_en: Pay for What You Want Repeated
scenario_en: Your $5-per-collected-check incentive worked great — until you notice your AR clerk asking customers to split payments into multiple checks, and steering effort toward easy small accounts while the big 90-day balances sit untouched.
option_a_en: Drop the incentive — it's clearly corrupting behavior.
option_b_en: Have a stern talk about the spirit of the program and leave the rules alone.
option_c_en: Redesign it: pay on dollars collected and aging reduction, not check count — reward exactly the outcome you want.
why_en: People do precisely what you pay for — that's the proof incentives work. Don't kill the engine; aim it. Pay for collected dollars and shrinking aging, and design against gaming from day one.
principle_voice_en: Design incentive plans with the explicit expectation that things WILL change — guard against gaming.

scenario_en: Your trusted bookkeeper of twelve years opens mail, enters bills, cuts checks, signs with the stamp, and reconciles the bank — everything. She's never taken a full vacation. The owner says, "Why insult her with controls? She's family."
option_a_en: Split the duties so fraud would require collusion, send bank statements to the owner's home, mandate vacations — and tell everyone the controls exist.
option_b_en: Agree — twelve loyal years has earned full trust.
option_c_en: Add a yearly CPA review but change nothing day-to-day.
why_en: Trust is not a control, and good systems protect honest people — they make the trusted bookkeeper un-accusable. Visible controls deter quietly; one unwatched hero is how every fraud story starts.
principle_voice_en: Every fraud story begins with 'I trusted them.

principle_title_en: How We Do Anything Is How We Do Everything
scenario_en: Year-end. Your chart of accounts has 240 accounts: duplicates, a "Misc" holding $11,000, dead accounts from a business line sold years ago. Reports still technically run. The owner preaches spotless trucks and spotless jobsites — then asks why financial reviews take so long.
option_a_en: Leave it — the CPA untangles it at tax time anyway.
option_b_en: Hide the dead accounts from report views so things look cleaner.
option_c_en: Clean it like a jobsite: merge duplicates, empty Misc to real accounts, retire dead accounts, match the SOE standard chart.
why_en: How we do anything is how we do everything. A company with spotless trucks and a junk-drawer chart of accounts is lying to itself somewhere. The standard is the standard — including in QuickBooks.
principle_voice_en: Thought applied even to mundane decisions — like a chart of accounts — pays forever.

scenario_en: Your Indeed ad has run for three weeks. Forty applicants, none qualified. Your Glassdoor sits at 2.4 stars, the trucks are dirty, and the ad reads "must have own tools, no whiners." The owner says, "The labor market is just terrible." You're staring at the repost button.
option_a_en: Raise the posted wage by $2 an hour and repost the same ad.
option_b_en: Fix what candidates actually see — the reviews, the ad's tone, the shop, the brand. Your applicants mirror your company.
option_c_en: Post the identical ad on three more job boards to widen the net.
why_en: The candidates you attract are a reflection of the company you built. More money or more boards just shows more people the same shadow. Change the company candidates see and the applicant pool changes with it.
principle_voice_en: You get the team you deserve.

scenario_en: Monday manager meeting. Three hires this year all washed out by month four. Around the table everyone nods at the same sentence: "Good people are just hard to find around here." It's becoming the company motto, and nobody has changed a single step of how you actually recruit.
option_a_en: Own it: audit your recruiting like a sales funnel — sourcing, screening, interviews, offers — and rebuild the weak steps.
option_b_en: Add a $1,500 signing bonus and hope better people show up.
option_c_en: Hand hiring to a staffing agency so the misses become their problem.
why_en: "Good people are hard to find" is a self-fulfilling excuse. Your results came from your process. Until you own that and change the inputs, you'll keep deserving the same washouts.
principle_voice_en: What percentage of the blame for the problems you have is you?

scenario_en: The tech you hired in a hurry quit in week three — right after gouging a customer's hardwood floor. Total damage: $4,800, one furious customer, one burned crew. The foreman wants someone to blame. You're embarrassed because you skipped two steps to get him on a truck faster.
option_a_en: Tell the team "this is why we can't have nice things" and get back to the schedule.
option_b_en: Swear off Indeed — that's where he came from, so the source is the problem.
option_c_en: Run a post-mortem on the hire, name the skipped steps, and turn the lesson into a permanent process upgrade.
why_en: A bad hire's damage is tuition — but only if you collect the lesson. Pain becomes fuel when it upgrades the process so the same mistake can't happen twice.
principle_voice_en: Your pain can be your poison or your fuel – you choose.

scenario_en: You've hired eleven people in your career and never once been taught how. Every interview is improvised. Slow season starts next month and you have two seats to fill — the first real breathing room you've had all year to get better at this.
option_a_en: Block weekly time to study hiring — books, audio in the truck, the SOE classes — and practice before the seats open.
option_b_en: Keep winging it; eleven hires of experience is the best teacher there is.
option_c_en: Copy a list of interview questions from the first Google result and call yourself trained.
why_en: People who stop learning reach the limits of what they already know. Recruiting is a learnable skill, and slow season is exactly when a learning machine builds the skill before it's needed.
principle_voice_en: What's easy to do is easy not to do.

scenario_en: Thirty-one applications sit in your inbox from last week's ad. Your office manager says, "We only call the good ones — calling everybody would eat half a day." It's busy season. You also know this is a small town where everyone talks, and half those applicants are someone's cousin or customer.
option_a_en: Agree with her — the schedule is slammed and unqualified applicants will never know the difference.
option_b_en: Call or message every single applicant within 48 hours, every time, no exceptions — and build it into the routine.
option_c_en: Set up an automatic rejection email so everyone at least hears something.
why_en: Calling every applicant back is a basic, and the basics are where the battle is won or lost. Every ignored applicant is a neighbor, a future customer, and a megaphone in a small town.
principle_voice_en: Become brilliant on the basics, because that is where the battle is won or lost.

scenario_en: The owner waves off your concern: "Our turnover's fine — people just leave for more money, that's the trade." You quietly pull the files: nine of the last fourteen hires left inside a year, and three exit notes mention the same supervisor. The owner wants your hiring report Friday.
option_a_en: Soften the numbers in the report so Friday's meeting doesn't blow up.
option_b_en: Go with the owner's story — he's been doing this thirty years and knows his company.
option_c_en: Calculate the real turnover rate and the real exit reasons, and present the facts straight.
why_en: You can't fix a problem you won't name. Honest turnover numbers and real exit reasons are the starting position — comfortable stories about "money" protect egos while the same supervisor empties the bench.
principle_voice_en: Facts do not cease to exist because they are ignored.

scenario_en: Your crew lead quit Friday afternoon. The owner wants interviews running Monday morning. There's no job description, no list of what made the last lead great — or what made the one before him a disaster. The recruiter asks, "So... what am I screening for, exactly?"
option_a_en: Spend two hours first defining the job, the ideal qualities, and what success looks like — then interview against that picture.
option_b_en: Start interviews Monday and figure out the role as candidates come through; speed matters.
option_c_en: Reuse the old install-tech ad — close enough, and it's already written.
why_en: Everything is created twice — once in the mind, once in reality. If you can't describe the right person before interviewing, you'll hire whoever shows up and call it fate. Two hours of design beats two months of regret.
principle_voice_en: You have to have a dream to make a dream come true.

scenario_en: Your top HVAC candidate calls: a competitor offered $1.50 more per hour. He's good — really good — and he's deciding by Friday. Your wage is fair but you can't win a pure bidding war, and your company has a training program, a growth path, and a story the competitor can't match.
option_a_en: Match the wage plus $2 and hope that ends it.
option_b_en: Sell the story — where the company is going, his growth path, the training, the why. Then talk total package.
option_c_en: Let him walk; if he chases nickels now, he'll chase them forever.
why_en: With strong enough reasons, people do incredible things — including taking the better career over the bigger hourly number. Sell the vision first; a wage-only win invites the next bidder to take him the same way.
principle_voice_en: If there is no why, the how doesn't matter.

scenario_en: The owner personally interviews every candidate — even part-time warehouse help. He's proud of it. He's also working seventy-hour weeks, and hiring freezes completely whenever he travels. Two candidates took other jobs last month while waiting for a slot on his calendar.
option_a_en: Schedule interviews at 7 p.m. so the owner can squeeze them in after the day job.
option_b_en: Pause hiring until slow season when the owner has more time.
option_c_en: Build a screening process the team runs end-to-end; the owner meets finalists only.
why_en: The business is supposed to serve its owner, not consume him. A hiring system the team runs gets candidates hired faster AND gives the owner his evenings back. Owner-as-bottleneck is the opposite of both.
principle_voice_en: You want your business to give you more of a life, not take more of your life.

principle_title_en: Do Right When It Costs You
scenario_en: Final interview with your best candidate in months. He asks directly: "Will I work Saturdays?" The truth: every Saturday from June through August, no exceptions. You can feel the offer dying in your hands if you say it plainly — and the seat has been open nine weeks.
option_a_en: Tell the whole truth — every summer Saturday — plus why, and how you make it fair with comp time and pay.
option_b_en: Say "occasionally" and let him discover the real schedule after he starts.
option_c_en: Dodge it: "Let's talk scheduling once we get you an offer."
why_en: An honest job preview costs you some candidates now; overpromising costs you the hire, the rework, and your name later. He'll learn the truth in June either way — the only question is whether you told it.
principle_voice_en: Tell the whole truth even when it's not pretty.

principle_title_en: Hiring Makes You or Breaks You
scenario_en: Busy season. A crew is down a man, the schedule is bleeding, and one candidate is available to start Monday. He's a warm body with a pulse and a vague resume. Your production manager is in your doorway: "I don't care who — I need somebody on that truck."
option_a_en: Hire him — trucks have to roll Monday, and you can always fix it later.
option_b_en: Hold the standard and keep recruiting hard; a wrong hire trades 1% recruiting effort for 99% managing mistakes.
option_c_en: Hire him as a "temporary" and decide what he really is later.
why_en: Hiring is the one job a manager must do really well. The warm body solves one week of schedule and creates months of callbacks, damage, and drama. Short a man hurts; wrong man breaks.
principle_voice_en: In 30 years I have never regretted firing someone (although I have regretted hiring many of the wrong people!)

scenario_en: A service-tech candidate aces your technical test — best you've ever seen. In the interview he trash-talks all three former employers, and one reference quietly says "wouldn't rehire." It's peak season, the board is full, and his skills would pay off the first week.
option_a_en: Hire him — talent like that is rare, and you can manage the attitude later.
option_b_en: Hire him on a 90-day probation as insurance.
option_c_en: Pass. Never hire negativity, no matter how skilled. Finish the background checks and restart the search.
why_en: Skill fixes pipes; character shapes the crew. Negativity spreads to every truck he rides in, and probation just schedules the damage. The references already told you the ending — believe them.
principle_voice_en: End gossip, negativity, and sabotage decisively.

scenario_en: Final round for a service manager seat that's been open six weeks. The candidate is... fine. Nobody on the panel is excited; nobody can name a real objection either. Someone shrugs: "He checks the boxes. Six weeks is a long time." The offer letter is drafted and waiting.
option_a_en: Restart the search. If nobody loves the candidate, it's a no — settling for a B player gets you C players next.
option_b_en: Send the offer; an open seat for six weeks is costing you more than a "fine" hire would.
option_c_en: Hire him now and quietly plan to upgrade the seat next year.
why_en: A team of people you're sure about beats higher talent you're lukewarm on. Managers multiply: a B hires C's. "Fine" in the interview is the best he'll ever look.
principle_voice_en: Show the same care hiring your 73rd employee as your 3rd.

scenario_en: Marcus was your most careful warehouse guy — inventory perfect for two years. You promoted him into dispatch, where the phones stack up and plans change every ten minutes. Six weeks in, he's drowning, snapping at drivers, and your office manager says, "I think we have to let him go."
option_a_en: Write him up — the seat is the seat, and dispatch is the job he accepted.
option_b_en: Move him back where his careful, steady style wins; match the person to the seat. Everybody is right for some job.
option_c_en: Send him to a high-energy seminar to fix his personality.
why_en: People have different styles, and one personality is ideal for one job and not another. Marcus didn't become a bad employee in six weeks — you moved a great one into the wrong seat.
principle_voice_en: One personality is ideal for one job and not another.

scenario_en: You finally landed a genuine winner — great references, great attitude. Day one, he was tossed on a truck with a grunt of "watch and learn." Week four, he looks average, asks nothing, and a buddy heard him say he's "not sure this place actually wants him to succeed."
option_a_en: Conclude you mis-hired and cut your losses early.
option_b_en: Tell the foreman to "keep an eye on him" and check back next month.
option_c_en: Build the onboarding you skipped: a mapped first 30 days, a named trainer, and scheduled check-ins — starting tomorrow.
why_en: A winner badly onboarded becomes a demotivated average guy — that's on the company, not him. Train deliberately or you'll "remove" people you actually hired right.
principle_voice_en: An environment that doesn't like mediocrity but accepts it gets mediocrity.

scenario_en: Your production manager runs crews two men short and complains daily. When you ask what he's doing about it, he says, "Hiring? That's HR's job — I run production." HR has sent him six resumes; he hasn't opened the folder. Meanwhile he knows every good tech in the county by name.
option_a_en: Coach him: every manager recruits. Bench-building goes into his weekly schedule like safety meetings — non-negotiable.
option_b_en: Have HR push him more resumes and follow up harder.
option_c_en: Recruit his techs for him yourself so it finally gets done right.
why_en: Recruiting isn't a department, it's a management duty. The manager who knows every good tech in the county is the best recruiter the company has — if his leader makes recruiting part of the job, not an interruption to it.
principle_voice_en: The only job that pays $250 an hour is the leader's, if you do it right.

scenario_en: Three months ago you handed all hiring to your new office manager and walked away relieved. You've never reviewed her process, sat in an interview, or asked a single question. Now two of her hires have flamed out, and the owner asks you, pointedly: "Who hired them?"
option_a_en: Take hiring back — clearly delegation failed.
option_b_en: Stay out of it; you delegated it, so the misses are hers to fix.
option_c_en: Stay accountable: review her process together, set checkpoints and numbers — because "who hired them" includes you.
why_en: Delegate authority, retain responsibility. Handing off hiring with zero review isn't delegation, it's abdication. The fix isn't grabbing it back or hiding — it's coaching the delegate inside a process you still own.
principle_voice_en: Delegate authority, retain responsibility.

scenario_en: Your new CSR is "underperforming" in month one — booking rate too low, says the report. You pull her offer letter: no metrics mentioned. Her week-one training: shadowing whoever was least busy. Nobody ever told her booked appointments were the job. Her manager wants a write-up today.
option_a_en: Approve the write-up — the metrics are posted on the wall, after all.
option_b_en: Set expectations first: the role's numbers in writing, reviewed together — then hold her accountable from there.
option_c_en: Lower the booking target until she finds her feet.
why_en: You can't hold someone accountable to expectations they never received. Accountability without expectations isn't management, it's ambush — and it starts in the offer letter and week one, not month two.
principle_voice_en: Expectation gaps lead to execution gaps. There is not a close second.

scenario_en: Your new installer's first day: nobody expected him at the door, no uniform in his size, no locker, and the owner walked past without a hello. At lunch he texted a friend: "Not sure about this place." You hear about it from his crew lead that evening.
option_a_en: Redesign day one for every hire: team told in advance, gear ready, a real welcome, lunch with the owner.
option_b_en: Hand him a $50 gift card tomorrow and apologize for the rough start.
option_c_en: Do nothing — installers care about the paycheck, not pageantry.
why_en: A first day says "you matter here" or "you're a body." He decided whether to stay long-term before his first paycheck. Recognition starts at hello — design it, don't leave it to luck.
principle_voice_en: Pretend every employee has a sign around their neck that says, 'Make me feel important.

principle_title_en: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool
scenario_en: Your best tech — six years, trains the rookies, customers ask for him — tells you straight: a competitor called offering $3 more per hour. He hasn't said yes. He came to you first, which took guts. He's standing in your office waiting to see what you do with that.
option_a_en: Beat the offer by $4 on the spot — problem solved.
option_b_en: Remind him what loyalty means and mention the non-solicit agreement.
option_c_en: Thank him for the honesty. Review his pay fairly AND show the love — growth path, recognition, real time with him.
why_en: Retention is love in action, and he just tested whether any exists. Money alone wins the auction until the next bid; love plus fair pay wins the person. Threats lose him by Friday.
principle_voice_en: When a great employee leaves, they have fired you as their boss.

principle_title_en: Give Away the Credit, Take the Blame
scenario_en: The plumber your assistant manager championed just quit after eight chaotic weeks. In the leadership meeting, eyes turn to her. She's bracing for it. You signed off on the hire too, and the truth is your screening process is two questions and a handshake — for everyone.
option_a_en: Let her own it publicly; she pushed for him, and accountability has to mean something.
option_b_en: Take the blame yourself, name the weak process as the real failure, and fix it with her.
option_c_en: Say "these things happen" and move to the next agenda item.
why_en: A failed hire is the process's fault before it's any person's. Leaders who take the blame and fix the system keep managers willing to recruit boldly; leaders who assign blame get managers who stop hiring.
principle_voice_en: Take the blame, give away the credit — your people will be more loyal and work harder for you.

principle_title_en: Never Act on One Side of a Story
scenario_en: A foreman candidate's resume says "ran $2M in projects" at his last company, and he tells a great story about why he left: "new owner, total chaos." He interviews beautifully. The seat's been empty five weeks, he can start Monday, and the references would take days to chase down.
option_a_en: Hire him — the interview is the real test, and references only say nice things anyway.
option_b_en: Hire him now but call references during his first week, just in case.
option_c_en: Verify before deciding: call the references, confirm the $2M claim, hear the other side of that exit.
why_en: A resume is one side of a story told by its author. There are two sides to every exit, and one sure way to take the wrong action is acting on incomplete information. Days of checking beats months of cleanup.
principle_voice_en: One sure way to take the wrong action is to act on incomplete or incorrect information.

scenario_en: Your week-two service tech showed up late twice and skipped Friday's toolbox meeting. His trainer mentions it almost as an aside: "Probably just settling in." He's talented, you fought to land him, and bringing it up now feels heavy-handed. It would be easier to see if a pattern forms.
option_a_en: Talk with him today — friendly, direct, expectations restated — while it's a wobble, not a habit.
option_b_en: Note it in his file and address everything at the 90-day review.
option_c_en: Wait two more weeks for a clearer pattern before saying anything.
why_en: Week two is when habits set. A five-minute conversation now is coaching; the same conversation in month six is a confrontation over a pattern you tolerated. Lit fuses don't put themselves out.
principle_voice_en: If you don't neglect small daily matters, large ones rarely come up.

principle_title_en: Culture Is When the Boss Leaves
scenario_en: Your highest-billing tech mocks the new guys, ignores the morning huddle, and calls safety checklists "babysitting" — but only when managers aren't around. Two promising recruits quit in their first month this quarter. One exit note read: "I saw who gets away with what here."
option_a_en: Pair new hires with better mentors and keep them away from him.
option_b_en: Confront the behavior and end it — change or go — because who you tolerate teaches everyone what's true here.
option_c_en: Leave it alone; he produces, and culture talk doesn't pay the bills.
why_en: Culture is what happens when the boss leaves the building, and your tolerated star IS the lesson new hires learn. Every recruiting dollar you spend pours into a bucket he's drilling holes in.
principle_voice_en: Culture is what happens when the boss leaves the building.

scenario_en: Your third installer this year just gave notice. The exit interview is on your calendar — conducted, as always, by the supervisor he's escaping. Last year's exit forms all say "better opportunity" in suspiciously similar handwriting. He told a coworker the truth, but he "doesn't want to burn a bridge."
option_a_en: Skip exit interviews — people never tell the truth on the way out anyway.
option_b_en: Keep the supervisor on it; he knows the department best.
option_c_en: Have a neutral person interview him, promise no retaliation, and protect every future exit the same way.
why_en: Exit truth only surfaces where it's safe to speak. An exit interview run by the problem produces fiction, and you're rehiring the same seat yearly because the real reason never reaches you.
principle_voice_en: To set things right you have to see things right.

scenario_en: Your recruiter fills sales seats fast — the owner watches that number. Production has begged for two installers for a month and gets the leftovers. Now jobs are backing up, customers are waiting three extra weeks, and the production manager has stopped even sending requisitions. "Why bother?"
option_a_en: Treat every department as recruiting's customer: one ranked pipeline driven by what the whole machine needs to serve customers.
option_b_en: Keep sales first — without sales there is no business.
option_c_en: Tell production to do its own recruiting since they're unhappy with yours.
why_en: The company is one department: customer service. Recruiting serves every gear, and a starved production team means customers wait — which strangles the same sales you were staffing. The machine needs every gear turning.
principle_voice_en: We all win or lose together, and the company is one department.

principle_title_en: Serve the Human, Not the House
scenario_en: A candidate emails you the night before his interview: his mother had a stroke; he needs to reschedule, again — the second time. Your office manager rolls her eyes: "Flag him as unreliable and move on. We have a stack of resumes." His application was the strongest of the batch.
option_a_en: Move on — life happens, but reliability is the job.
option_b_en: Treat him like a human first: reschedule with genuine kindness, judge him on the interview, not the emergency.
option_c_en: Keep him in the pile but quietly rank him last.
why_en: Candidates are humans, not resumes. A family crisis isn't a reliability score. How you treat someone at their worst moment tells him — and everyone he talks to — exactly what working for you would be like.
principle_voice_en: We are not servicing a house, we are servicing a human being.

scenario_en: Your interviews happen in the break room — sticky table, fluorescent hum, interruptions every five minutes. Candidates wait twenty minutes past their slot. Yesterday a great electrician ghosted his second interview. His one-line reply to your follow-up text: "Took another offer. No hard feelings."
option_a_en: Accept it as tradesman behavior — ghosting goes both ways these days.
option_b_en: Add a $500 signing bonus to your ads to offset the experience.
option_c_en: Treat candidates like customers: on time, prepared room, shop tour, follow-up same day. Wow them — the interview IS marketing.
why_en: Candidates judge the job by the interview the way customers judge the work by the experience. A sloppy hiring experience tells your best prospect everything — and your best prospects have options.
principle_voice_en: Everything counts — customers and employees alike read every detail as evidence of who you are.

principle_title_en: The Experience Is Half the Product
scenario_en: A candidate applied Tuesday. Your system: application sits three days, then a generic email, then a phone screen "when someone gets to it." Average time to offer: 19 days. Your competitor texts applicants within an hour and interviews within 48. You keep losing the good ones in between.
option_a_en: Redesign the hiring journey like Moments of Truth — map every touch point, set speed standards, make the process itself sell the company.
option_b_en: Tell candidates upfront that good things take time — quality companies move carefully.
option_c_en: Skip the screening steps entirely and jump straight to offers to beat the competitor's speed.
why_en: The hiring process is the company's first Moment of Truth — candidates infer what working here is like from how applying here feels. Slow and silent reads as "this is how they'll treat me." Speed up the touches, not past the standards.
principle_voice_en: Great companies leave nothing to chance.

scenario_en: A fired installer posted a one-star Indeed review: "Management plays favorites, promises are garbage." It's half false, a little true, and now it's the first thing every applicant reads. Your ops manager wants to reply hot and "set the record straight." Applications dipped this week.
option_a_en: Have the lawyer demand Indeed remove it.
option_b_en: Respond publicly with grace — own what's fair, correct facts calmly, invite a direct conversation — and fix the kernel of truth.
option_c_en: Ignore it; responding only feeds the fire, and reviews blow over.
why_en: Every applicant reads the review AND your reply. A graceful, honest response turns the attack into proof of character; a hot one proves his point. Problems are tests — this one is public, and you can pass it.
principle_voice_en: Act fast and take responsibility before bad news hits the internet forever.

scenario_en: Dana, a solid tech who left two years ago on good terms for a bigger shop, just liked your company's Facebook post. Word is she's unhappy where she landed. Your old policy — unwritten but real — is "we don't take people back." You have a seat she could fill in her sleep.
option_a_en: Stand by the policy — taking back leavers teaches everyone the grass is greener.
option_b_en: Wait for her to apply; reaching out first looks desperate.
option_c_en: Call her this week. Boomerang hires come trained, proven, and humble — and build an alumni bench that never closes.
why_en: Keep your people for life the way you keep customers for life. A good leaver who returns is your cheapest, safest, fastest hire — and every alumnus treated warmly becomes a recruiter in someone else's shop.
principle_voice_en: The best people are already working somewhere — keep in touch before you need them.

scenario_en: You're about to call your finalist with the offer. Your plan: email the comp sheet and "let him think it over." He's also interviewing at two other shops. You know this job genuinely fits his goals — he said so himself — but pushing feels pushy, and you hate feeling like a salesperson.
option_a_en: Treat the offer call like a close: connect the offer to his goals, ask for the yes, handle hesitations live. Recruiting IS selling.
option_b_en: Email the offer with a one-week deadline and wait respectfully.
option_c_en: Lowball slightly to leave room for the negotiation you're dreading.
why_en: If the job truly fits his goals, helping him say yes is a service, not pressure. An emailed offer left to "think it over" hands your finalist to whichever competitor actually asks for the business.
principle_voice_en: Sell 'em! It's the right thing to do for everyone!

scenario_en: Three finalists for an apprentice seat: a chatty kid who "feels like a fit," a quiet career-changer from retail management, and a woman who'd be the first female installer your crews have had. Your foreman has already decided: "The kid. The other two won't last in this trade."
option_a_en: Trust the foreman's gut — he's the one who has to work with them.
option_b_en: Run all three through the same scorecard, work sample, and ride-along — and judge only the evidence.
option_c_en: Compromise and drop just the retail guy; no trade background is a real gap.
why_en: Pre-judging filters out exactly the people nobody else is smart enough to hire — the quiet ones, the career-changers, the firsts. Evidence from the same test for everyone beats a foreman's hunch about who "lasts."
principle_voice_en: Include people unlike you who complement your weaknesses.

scenario_en: Phone screen, ninety seconds in, the candidate asks: "What's it pay?" Your recruiter's habit is to blurt the range and watch half of them hang up. This candidate is exactly the experienced foreman you've hunted for months — and your base wage is mid-market, though the whole package isn't.
option_a_en: Quote the base wage immediately — transparency, take it or leave it.
option_b_en: Refuse to discuss money until the final interview.
option_c_en: Sell the career first — growth, training, culture, total package — then put the wage inside that picture.
why_en: A wage quoted before value is built is just a number to compare against someone else's number. Mid-market base inside a great career story wins; mid-market base alone loses in ninety seconds.
principle_voice_en: Once they have the price they don't need you anymore.

scenario_en: The best foreman in your market turned you down fourteen months ago — happy where he is. You crossed him off. Today his company just got bought by a private-equity roll-up, and your superintendent mentions he "didn't sound thrilled" at the supply house this morning.
option_a_en: Leave him be — chasing a guy who said no looks desperate and burns goodwill.
option_b_en: Call him today with the news as your reason — and put him on a bench list you touch every quarter, forever.
option_c_en: Wait for him to reach out; he knows where to find you.
why_en: "No" means "not yet." Great people working elsewhere are the bench — court them for years with real touches, and be the first call when their world changes. Today their world changed.
principle_voice_en: I WILL KEEP FOLLOWING UP – FOREVER, UNTIL THE SALE IS MADE.

scenario_en: The owner just slashed your recruiting budget: "Ads, assessments, reference services — $9,000 a year we don't need." Meanwhile, last year's two mis-hires cost roughly $40,000 each in wages, training hours, truck damage, redone work, and one lost customer — numbers nobody has ever put in front of him.
option_a_en: Show him the math: the full cost of a wrong hire versus the cost of hiring right. Recruiting spend is cash protection.
option_b_en: Accept the cut and quietly run a thinner process; you'll make it work.
option_c_en: Shift the savings into signing bonuses since those at least attract bodies.
why_en: Cash is life, and nothing burns it quieter than a wrong hire — wages, rework, damage, churned customers. $9,000 of process that prevents one $40,000 mistake is the best margin in the building. Show the math.
principle_voice_en: Being busy growing the company and not watching the numbers is like stepping on the gas and closing your eyes.

scenario_en: The owner asks, "How's our hiring going?" Your honest answer would be "feels better lately." You track nothing: no turnover rate, no average tenure, no time-to-fill, no revenue per employee. Your competitor across town reportedly recites his numbers from memory at every leadership meeting.
option_a_en: Keep managing by feel — recruiting is about people, and people aren't spreadsheets.
option_b_en: Pull just this quarter's hires-versus-exits as a quick snapshot for the owner.
option_c_en: Build the dashboard — turnover rate, average tenure, time-to-fill, revenue per employee — and track it over years, not quarters.
why_en: All human business activity comes out to a number, and you must measure to know, compare, improve, and set goals. "Feels better" isn't a trend; five years of tracked turnover and tenure is.
principle_voice_en: You must measure to know, compare, improve, and set goals.

principle_title_en: Pay for What You Want Repeated
scenario_en: Your referral program pays $300 the day a referred hire starts. Techs have learned the game: refer anyone with a pulse, collect, shrug when the guy quits in week six. Meanwhile your best installer brought in two five-year keepers and got the same $300 as everybody else.
option_a_en: Kill the program — it's clearly being gamed beyond saving.
option_b_en: Restructure it: bigger money, paid in stages at 90 days and one year — pay for retention, the thing you actually want.
option_c_en: Raise the bonus to $600 at start so referrals at least keep flowing.
why_en: Behavior follows the bonus. Pay at day one and you've bought warm bodies; pay at ninety days and a year and you've bought keepers. Reward exactly what you want repeated — nothing else.
principle_voice_en: What gets tracked and celebrated gets improved.

scenario_en: Your ops manager is famous for his gut: "I know a good tech in five minutes." His record says otherwise — roughly half his five-minute hires washed out. He skips the phone screen, freelances his questions, and never uses the ride-along working interview. He hires again next week.
option_a_en: Install the system: same questions for everyone, multi-step screening, a working ride-along — no gut-only hires, including his.
option_b_en: Let him keep his method but ask him to jot notes afterward for the file.
option_c_en: Pair his gut with yours — two guts interviewing together should cancel the errors.
why_en: A coin flips half-heads too. Scripts and repeatable steps make excellence repeatable for ordinary people; gut-only hiring makes results depend on a hero having a good day. Same process, every candidate, every time.
principle_voice_en: There are so many benefits from a simple idea executed well!

principle_title_en: How We Do Anything Is How We Do Everything
scenario_en: Tomorrow your best candidate in a year tours the shop. Right now: overflowing trash, a dead truck on blocks, last month's safety poster on the floor, and a break room that smells like 2019. Your supervisor laughs: "He's applying to turn wrenches, not judge feng shui."
option_a_en: Tour him through the office only and keep the shop doors closed.
option_b_en: Apologize in advance — "excuse the mess, busy season" — and tour as-is.
option_c_en: Clean it tonight and keep it that way — the shop tells candidates exactly how you do everything else.
why_en: Everything employees and candidates see teaches. A messy shop says "this is our standard" louder than any pitch — and how you keep the shop is how you'll keep your promises to him. Details are evidence.
principle_voice_en: We are ladies and gentlemen serving ladies and gentlemen.

scenario_en: Year-end review at the foundation repair company you run: crews leave messy jobsites, the office returns calls late, sales meetings start whenever. The owner brought in a consultant, who quietly points out that you skip training nights, roll in at 9:30, and your own truck is a disaster. He asks, "Where do you think they learned it?"
option_a_en: Hire a tough operations manager to tighten everyone up — you'll focus on growth.
option_b_en: Audit yourself first: your punctuality, your truck, your training attendance. Change you, then re-set the standard.
option_c_en: Send a company-wide memo on standards with discipline for the next violation.
why_en: The business is your reflection and will never outperform its leader. Hiring an enforcer or sending memos while you model sloppiness just teaches everyone the memo is optional.
principle_voice_en: Your business is your elongated shadow.

scenario_en: A $14,000 drainage install failed and flooded the customer's basement. The installer you hired in a rush — no process, two days of shadowing, no checklist — skipped the test you never taught him. The customer is furious and your sales manager says, "Fire the guy and tell her it was one bad apple."
option_a_en: Fire the installer, tell the customer a bad apple is gone, move on.
option_b_en: Write him up, retrain him, and call it a shared mistake.
option_c_en: Own it fully: you hired him, you trained him, you set the expectations. Fix her basement, then fix your hiring and training system.
why_en: Total responsibility. The bad-apple story is the convenient lie — the system that produced him is still running and will produce another one next month.
principle_voice_en: I hired them, I trained them, I set the expectations, I created the culture, so I am responsible.

scenario_en: Brutal February: your biggest commercial account left, your second-best salesperson quit for the competitor who poached him, and you're at the kitchen table at 11 p.m. replaying both losses. Tomorrow morning the team will read your face. You can feel yourself turning bitter.
option_a_en: Write down what you control — inputs, mentors, books, the plan — and convert the sting into a 90-day counterattack.
option_b_en: Bury it, say nothing, and grind longer hours until the numbers cover it.
option_c_en: Open Monday's meeting venting about disloyal employees and an unfair market.
why_en: Setbacks are poison or fuel — you choose. Grinding in silence changes nothing upstream; venting poisons the whole shop. Changing your inputs changes everything downstream.
principle_voice_en: Your pain can be your poison or your fuel – you choose.

scenario_en: You're in the 60-hour-week trap. A three-day leadership workshop you've wanted for two years lands in April — your busy season — and costs $3,000 plus travel. Your operations manager says, "We can't lose you for three days." You haven't read a business book since 2023.
option_a_en: Skip it. The business needs you on deck during the busy season.
option_b_en: Send your operations manager instead and have him report back what he learned.
option_c_en: Go yourself. Prepare the team, take the three days, and come back a better leader.
why_en: Work harder on yourself than on your job — the leader is the lid on the company. Sending your ops manager looks like development, but the constraint you're avoiding upgrading is you.
principle_voice_en: Entrepreneurship is the power to create. First, the power to create yourself.

scenario_en: Sales are slipping. Digging in, you find your reps quietly stopped same-day written proposals — "we email them later to save time" — and most ask for the business once, if at all. The same week, a vendor pitches you a hot new lead-generation channel with a slick demo.
option_a_en: Buy the new lead channel — more at-bats will cover the slippage.
option_b_en: Re-install the basics first: same-day written proposals, presented in person, three asks, full effort on every lead.
option_c_en: Drop prices 10% to close more of what you're already running.
why_en: Simple things done without fail win the battle. Pouring expensive new leads into a team that abandoned the basics just wastes them faster — and discounting punishes margin for a discipline problem.
principle_voice_en: What's easy to do is easy not to do.

scenario_en: You tell everyone you run "a $4 million company." The real number: $2.9M installed, margin down two points, and your closing ratio trails the peer group you met at a conference. The owner wants a growth plan on his desk by Friday. Your ego wants the $4M story in it.
option_a_en: Build the plan on the real numbers, benchmark against peers, and ask on paper: "What percentage of the blame is me?"
option_b_en: Present optimistic projections to keep the owner confident.
option_c_en: Hold a morale rally first — the team needs belief before bad news.
why_en: To set things right you have to see things right. A plan built on a flattering story fails in the field; a rally before reality is anesthesia, not leadership.
principle_voice_en: What percentage of the blame for the problems you have is you?

scenario_en: The owner wants a second installation crew next year — roughly $1M more capacity — and the plan is yours to build. At an auction Saturday, a clean box truck goes cheap. Your foreman says grab it; the owner asks what the actual plan is. You have a feeling, a goal number, and nothing on paper.
option_a_en: Post a help-wanted ad now and figure out the rest as it comes.
option_b_en: Push the owner to grab the truck — the deal forces everyone to commit.
option_c_en: Model it first — functional, financial, physical: the leads, the numbers, the people and equipment — then close the gap block by block.
why_en: Everything is created twice — first in the mind, then in reality. The truck feels decisive, but it's a physical answer to a question you haven't finished asking. Planning flushes out the problems for free.
principle_voice_en: You have to have a dream to make a dream come true.

scenario_en: At the all-hands you unveil "$10 million by 2029!" Eyes glaze. Afterward your sales manager asks privately, "Why ten? What does it do for anyone in that room?" You realize your honest answer is "because we can." The plan binder is thick; the reason is missing.
option_a_en: Break the goal into department quotas — clarity will create buy-in.
option_b_en: Stop. Define the why — for you, for them, for customers — then relaunch the goal connected to what people actually care about.
option_c_en: Attach bonus money to the number and let cash do the talking.
why_en: Reasons come first, answers second. Quotas and bonuses are "how" machinery; nobody pushes through hard Februarys for a number that only makes the owner richer.
principle_voice_en: If there is no why, the how doesn't matter.

scenario_en: You haven't taken a real vacation in three years. Your spouse books a week at the shore in July — the same week as your biggest install of the summer. Your production manager is capable but has never run a big job without you hovering. The deposit on the beach house is non-refundable.
option_a_en: Go. Brief the team, give your production manager full authority, and treat the week as the independence test.
option_b_en: Postpone the trip to the slow season — just this one more time.
option_c_en: Go, but run the job by phone from the beach all week.
why_en: The business exists to give you more of a life, not take more of it. "One more time" is how three years became three more. A team that can't run a week without you is the real emergency.
principle_voice_en: You want your business to give you more of a life, not take more of your life.

principle_title_en: Do Right When It Costs You
scenario_en: Your estimator mis-measured a signed $18,000 waterproofing job; done right, you'll lose about $2,500. Payroll is Friday and February was slow. The easy out is a quick call: "Material costs jumped — the price has to go up." The customer would probably believe it.
option_a_en: Make the material-costs call and re-price the job.
option_b_en: Tell the customer the truth and ask to split the difference.
option_c_en: Keep your word, do the job as signed, eat the loss — then fix the measuring process.
why_en: Your word is the product. The fudged call is convenient and probably works once — and makes you a company that lies when it's expensive. The system fix makes the $2,500 tuition, not waste.
principle_voice_en: If people don't believe the messenger, they won't believe the message.

principle_title_en: Hiring Makes You or Breaks You
scenario_en: Production backlog hits six weeks and your best foreman is begging for help. A warm body walked in today — available Monday, vague résumé, "lots of experience." Your full hiring process — interviews, references, background, working interview — takes three weeks you don't feel you have.
option_a_en: Hire him Monday. Bodies now, sorting later.
option_b_en: Keep the process. Bridge the gap with six-day weeks and helpers around your strong foremen while you recruit right.
option_c_en: Skip references and background — one good interview and he starts Wednesday.
why_en: 95% of success is the people you choose. The rushed hire converts a six-week scheduling problem into a multi-year managing-your-mistake problem. Flex capacity buys the time the process needs.
principle_voice_en: Hiring will make you, or break you. Too often contractors spend 1% of their time recruiting and 99% of their time managing their recruiting mistakes.

scenario_en: A candidate just aced your working interview — genuinely the best technical installer you've ever watched. Then both reference calls hint at the same things: side jobs with company customers and constant badmouthing of his last boss. Your production manager says, "We can keep an eye on him. Look at those hands."
option_a_en: Pass. Restart the search, and tell your manager exactly why.
option_b_en: Hire him with a stern zero-tolerance warning on day one.
option_c_en: Use him as a subcontractor so the risk stays outside the company.
why_en: You can teach skills; you can't teach character. Two references singing the same song is data, not gossip. The subcontractor dodge still puts his character in your customers' homes wearing your reputation.
principle_voice_en: We don't get people to adopt our core values. We find people who already have them.

scenario_en: The sales manager seat has been empty four months and it's costing you. After final interviews you grade the best of three finalists a 7.5 out of 10 — solid résumé, fine answers, no spark. Your team liked him "okay." Recruiting again means two more months of you covering the job.
option_a_en: Hire the 7.5 — perfect is the enemy of good, and the seat is bleeding.
option_b_en: Promote your top salesperson tonight to stop the pain.
option_c_en: Restart the search. If you don't love the candidate, the answer is no.
why_en: A players hire A players; a "fine" leader hire caps every hire under him. The 7.5 feels responsible — that's the trap. Two more hard months beat three mediocre years.
principle_voice_en: Sometimes the best hiring decision is the one not to hire.

scenario_en: Your office manager is brilliant with systems, schedules, and numbers — and after a year of coaching, still stiff and short with upset customers on the phone. Yesterday she made a crying customer angrier. She's loyal, ten years in, and knows the job description says phones are hers.
option_a_en: Keep coaching the phones — leaders don't give up on people.
option_b_en: Redesign the seats: give her systems and accounting fully, and hire a natural service-giver for the phones.
option_c_en: Write her up — the phones are in her job description.
why_en: Put strengths where they're valued and weaknesses where they don't matter. A year of coaching against wiring isn't loyalty, it's friction for her and the customer. Everybody is right for some seat.
principle_voice_en: Everybody is right for some job.

scenario_en: Your installer of nine years — godfather to your foreman's kid, a fixture at the Christmas party — has slipped for six months: callbacks, shortcuts, two warranty claims. You've had two friendly chats. Nothing changed. The crew has started quietly redoing his work, and the busy season starts in three weeks.
option_a_en: Build a written training plan with clear standards and a 30-day deadline — improve, or part ways with dignity.
option_b_en: Keep covering. Nine years buys patience; it'll probably come around.
option_c_en: Quietly move him to shop duties without naming the real issue.
why_en: Hope is not a strategy. Knowing what you now know, you wouldn't hire today's version of him — so train him back to hireable or release him with dignity. The quiet shuffle dodges the truth he deserves.
principle_voice_en: In 30 years I have never regretted firing someone (although I have regretted hiring many of the wrong people!)

scenario_en: Your best salesperson is out six weeks for surgery, leaving $400K of pipeline uncovered. Fifteen years ago you were the best closer in the county, and part of you is thrilled at the excuse. Your two remaining reps are average. Your calendar as GM is already full of the work only you can do.
option_a_en: Run his leads yourself — nobody in the building closes like you.
option_b_en: Split the leads and cut marketing spend to shrink the pipeline to fit.
option_c_en: Redistribute the leads and use six weeks of ride-alongs to coach your average reps up. Stay in the leader seat.
why_en: You're paid for the team's results, not yours. Taking the bag back feels heroic and pays you wages while your real job — building doers — goes undone for six weeks.
principle_voice_en: Freedom doesn't come when you've solved all your problems. Freedom comes when you realize you can't do it alone.

scenario_en: Three months ago you handed marketing to a new manager with one instruction: "Make the phone ring." No budget, no lead targets, no weekly review. Leads are down 20% and he seems busy but lost. You're embarrassed, swamped, and the spring push starts in six weeks.
option_a_en: Own the bad handoff. Re-delegate properly — purpose, lead goals, budget, weekly reporting — and coach him to the targets.
option_b_en: Take marketing back yourself until things stabilize.
option_c_en: Give him another quarter to figure it out — you're too busy right now.
why_en: "Make the phone ring" was abdication, and abdication's failures belong to you. Taking it back keeps the job forever; another blind quarter is the convenient version of the same mistake.
principle_voice_en: If you never give authority away, you'll keep the job forever. Is that what you want?

scenario_en: You discover three internet leads sat unanswered overnight — at $200 a lead, $600 burned while a competitor called those homeowners back in minutes. You're furious and halfway to writing up the appointment center rep. Then you check: there is no written speed-to-lead standard anywhere. There never has been.
option_a_en: Write up the rep — anyone with sense knows leads can't sit.
option_b_en: Set the explicit standard first — every inquiry answered inside the hour, scripts, coverage, training — then hold people to it.
option_c_en: Install monitoring software so you can catch the slackers yourself.
why_en: Expectation gaps cause execution gaps — there's no close second. Punishing people for standards that live only in your head teaches fear; surveillance without clarity teaches distrust. Clarity first, accountability second.
principle_voice_en: Expectation gaps lead to execution gaps. There is not a close second.

scenario_en: Budget night. The office is whispering about raises, morale feels flat, and exit interviews say people feel invisible. Meanwhile your best foreman just finished a brutal ten-day job flawlessly, in the rain — and nobody above him said one word about it. You have $15K of discretionary room, total.
option_a_en: Spread it as across-the-board 3% raises — money talks.
option_b_en: Hold it for a December bonus announcement.
option_c_en: Start recognizing now: call the foreman tonight, handwritten notes, public praise at the rally — and keep the cash for targeted rewards.
why_en: People do more for recognition than for money. A 3% raise is forgotten by the second paycheck; a specific, public, genuine thank-you goes on the garage wall for ten years.
principle_voice_en: Pretend every employee has a sign around their neck that says, 'Make me feel important.

principle_title_en: Love Is the Greatest Leadership Tool
scenario_en: Your dispatcher — five years, rock solid — has been distracted for a month: double-booked crews twice, snapped at a foreman. Friday you learn her mother is seriously ill three states away. She hasn't asked for anything. Monday's schedule is the busiest of the year, and she builds it.
option_a_en: Meet privately, ask about her mom, and build the help together — flex schedule, covered days, whatever family needs.
option_b_en: Quietly route her error-prone tasks to others until it passes.
option_c_en: Document the errors now so the company is protected either way.
why_en: Helping with life is love, and people who know you care become their own supervisors. The quiet workaround looks gentle but tells her she's a risk, not a person — and solves nothing she's carrying.
principle_voice_en: In the end it comes down to: do you love people?

principle_title_en: Give Away the Credit, Take the Blame
scenario_en: Record quarter — best in company history — driven mostly by a pricing change your young sales manager pushed for over your objections. The trade association invites you to tell the story on stage, and a reporter from the county business journal wants "the GM's secret." Meanwhile, the one blemish this quarter, a botched install, was technically his scheduling call too.
option_a_en: Tell the story straight: his idea, your initial doubt, team execution — and own the botched install as your miss.
option_b_en: Take the stage yourself but thank "the whole team" in general.
option_c_en: Share credit for the win and let him explain the install failure — accountability matters.
why_en: Credit flows down, blame flows up. The vague "whole team" thank-you quietly keeps the spotlight on you, and pinning the blemish on him while pocketing his win is exactly backwards.
principle_voice_en: In a rally speech, the leader gives away all the credit, and takes all the blame.

principle_title_en: Never Act on One Side of a Story
scenario_en: Your office manager — fifteen years, trusted completely — corners you Friday: "Your new production manager screamed at Maria and she's about to quit. You need to deal with him today." It's the third complaint she's brought you about him this month. He's been changing how the office schedules crews, and you know she hated losing that control.
option_a_en: Act on it today — three complaints from your most trusted person is enough evidence.
option_b_en: Tell the production manager to apologize and slow his changes down.
option_c_en: Talk to him, Maria, and anyone who was there before judging — and notice who benefits if he loses.
why_en: There's a story behind the story — sometimes the accuser is defending turf. Trusted people can still weaponize your bias for action. One sure way to act wrong is to act on one side.
principle_voice_en: One sure way to take the wrong action is to act on incomplete or incorrect information.

scenario_en: Sunday night, your foreman texts: a crew nicked a gas line Friday at the Hendersons'. They smelled nothing, capped it themselves, said nothing, and finished the job. The utility hasn't inspected it. The customer is happy and has already posted a glowing review. Calling means an awkward conversation, a utility visit, and maybe a redone wall.
option_a_en: Call the customer and the utility first thing Monday, get it inspected, own it, and eat whatever it costs.
option_b_en: Say nothing — it's capped, it's fine, and reopening it only creates alarm.
option_c_en: Send the foreman back quietly "to check his work" without telling the customer why.
why_en: Crises are small problems someone decided to sit on. Silence is the convenient bet that compounds into the lawsuit, the headline, the lost license. Own it before the internet — or worse — does.
principle_voice_en: Good leaders recognize when a fuse is lit and act right away.

principle_title_en: Culture Is When the Boss Leaves
scenario_en: Your no-gossip rule is posted on the wall. Your best installer — fastest hands, customers love him, booked solid — is also the shop's gossip engine; you've now heard him trashing a new helper twice, and the helper looks ready to quit. Last guy you corrected for gossip was a junior tech. Everyone is watching what happens when it's the star.
option_a_en: Let it ride through the busy season — you can't afford to rattle your best producer right now.
option_b_en: Correct him privately, same standard as the junior tech, with clear consequences if it continues — star or not.
option_c_en: Re-announce the no-gossip policy at the next meeting without naming anyone.
why_en: Culture is what happens when you leave the building, and one tolerated violation rewrites the real rules for everyone. The unnamed announcement tells the shop the star is exempt — which is the lesson they'll keep.
principle_voice_en: An environment that doesn't like mediocrity but accepts it gets mediocrity.

scenario_en: Your last three good ideas all flopped quietly — and you found out months late each time. At today's manager meeting you floated a new commission plan and got six nods, zero questions. Later you overhear two managers in the yard listing exactly why it won't work. Neither said a word in the room. One used to push back, years ago — until a meeting where you tore his idea apart.
option_a_en: Confront the two managers about going behind your back.
option_b_en: Ask your brother-in-law manager to be your eyes and report what people really think.
option_c_en: Own the silence you created: admit the torn-apart moment, ask each manager privately "what's wrong with my plan?" — and reward the first hard answer.
why_en: The higher you climb, the worse your feedback — and you taught them silence. Punishing the yard conversation seals the vault; a spy network is a workaround for trust you have to rebuild yourself.
principle_voice_en: What can I start doing, stop doing and keep doing to be better for you?

scenario_en: Open warfare: production says sales "promises fantasy schedules to close deals"; sales says production "kills referrals with sloppy handoffs." A customer just got caught in the crossfire — told two different start dates a week apart. Your sales and production managers each want a meeting with you, separately, to blame the other.
option_a_en: Put both managers in one room: there is one department here — customer service. Build the shared handoff standard and a joint weekly meeting, together.
option_b_en: Meet each separately, hear both sides, and rule on who's right.
option_c_en: Add a coordinator role to sit between the two departments.
why_en: Us-vs-them is the disease; refereeing it or hiring a buffer feeds it. Each gear's output is the next gear's input — they serve each other or the customer pays. The unifier makes the lines disappear.
principle_voice_en: No matter where you work, there is one department — the customer service department.

principle_title_en: Serve the Human, Not the House
scenario_en: Ride-along day. Your top crew finishes a crawl space job technically perfect — and you watch them walk past the 80-year-old widow homeowner three times without a word. She trails them with questions; they answer in grunts, pack up, leave. The work is flawless. She looks rattled. Your foreman shrugs: "Job's done right, isn't it?"
option_a_en: Let it go — flawless work is what she paid for, and these guys produce.
option_b_en: Coach the crew that night: the human is the customer, not the house — then train greetings, check-ins, and the final walkthrough as standard.
option_c_en: Send her a gift card to smooth it over and move on.
why_en: Same product, different service, two different results. She can't judge the crawl space; she can judge how she was treated — and that's what she'll tell her neighbors. The gift card patches one symptom and trains nobody.
principle_voice_en: We are not servicing a house, we are servicing a human being who owns the home.

scenario_en: Your cost per lead has crept to $310 and your marketing manager wants another $40K for ads. Digging into the numbers, you notice referral leads — nearly free, closing at twice the rate — have fallen from 30% of volume to 12% over two years, the same period your post-job follow-up calls and little extras quietly died as you got busy.
option_a_en: Approve the $40K — leads are leads and the season is coming.
option_b_en: Cut prices to convert the expensive leads at a higher rate.
option_c_en: Rebuild the Wow engine first — follow-up calls, extras, referral program — and make exceeding expectations the measured standard again.
why_en: The flywheel runs Wow → referrals → cheaper leads → better margins → better people. You're paying $40K to outrun a broken flywheel. Merely satisfied customers tell no one; thrilled ones are your cheapest marketing department.
principle_voice_en: Satisfied customers call it a fair transaction and tell no one — thrill them so they become disciples who refer.

principle_title_en: The Experience Is Half the Product
scenario_en: Mystery-shopping your own company rattles you: the phone got answered on the sixth ring, the confirmation email had a typo, the salesman was great, the crew showed up 40 minutes early to a surprised customer in her bathrobe, and nobody called after completion. Five touchpoints, one good one. Your installs themselves are genuinely excellent.
option_a_en: Circulate the findings and tell each department to tighten up its piece.
option_b_en: Map every Moment of Truth start to finish, design on purpose what happens at each, and train and measure it.
option_c_en: Focus on install quality — that's the product they actually pay for.
why_en: Customers can't judge the install; they judge the experience and infer the work from it — and they roll every touchpoint into one verdict. "Tighten up" without design leaves the experience to whoever answers the phone.
principle_voice_en: Anyone can do the work, but not anyone provides a great Customer Experience.

scenario_en: Saturday, 7:40 a.m., your cell rings: a $30K basement job from last month is leaking onto new carpet, and the customer is loud, maybe unfair — your foreman swears the leak is from her gutter, not your system. Your service tech is off until Tuesday. She's threatening a review. Your weekend was supposed to be your kid's tournament.
option_a_en: Get someone there today — you if needed — fix first, sort out whose fault later.
option_b_en: Calmly explain it's likely her gutters and book Tuesday's first slot.
option_c_en: Offer a $500 goodwill credit by phone and schedule a visit for the week.
why_en: Problems are tests, and speed is the apology — "today" says you're on it; Tuesday says you're dodging. Right-or-wrong is irrelevant in hour one; a customer handled fast often refers more than one who never had a problem.
principle_voice_en: The only side of the story that counts is the customer's side.

scenario_en: Budget meeting. You have $25K left for the year. Option one: a new-customer ad blitz at roughly $250 per lead. Option two: your service manager's pitch — an annual maintenance-and-inspection program touching all 3,100 past customers, who currently never hear from you again after final payment. Your marketing manager calls past customers "done deals."
option_a_en: Split the money to keep both managers happy.
option_b_en: Take the blitz — growth comes from new names in the funnel.
option_c_en: Fund the annual-contact program — past customers are gold you already paid to mine.
why_en: Past customers know you, trust you, don't shop you, and cost a fraction to re-engage — and the annual visit generates leads, referrals, and reviews forever. "Done deals" is how you let gold walk to your competitor.
principle_voice_en: You have a choice – let them go or keep them forever.

scenario_en: Your service tech mentions that on a maintenance visit he noticed the customer's sump system is fifteen years old and one storm from failing — but said nothing, because "I'm not a salesman, and I didn't want to seem pushy." Two weeks later that customer's basement floods. She calls, upset: "Your guy was just here. Why didn't he tell me?"
option_a_en: Tighten the line: techs report findings to the office, and sales decides who to contact.
option_b_en: Train everybody that informing customers of real problems IS the help — with permission-based language and demonstration, never pressure.
option_c_en: Coach the tech privately and apologize to the customer with a discount.
why_en: Everybody sells, and failing to tell her was robbing her, not respecting her. The tech in the home has more credibility than any salesperson. The routing fix buries the moment of trust in paperwork.
principle_voice_en: Sell 'em! It's the right thing to do for everyone!

scenario_en: Monday's board has two appointments and one interview. Lead one: a rusted-gate farmhouse your salesman wants to skip — "they can't afford us; give me the lake house instead." The interview: a candidate who's driven a forklift for nine years, no industry experience, whose cover letter is the hungriest thing you've read all year. Your sales manager wants to cancel the farmhouse and skip the interview.
option_a_en: Run the farmhouse lead full-effort and hold the interview — judge people by behavior, not packaging.
option_b_en: Trust your salesman's read — he knows his territory.
option_c_en: Send the new guy to the farmhouse so your closer gets the lake house.
why_en: Pre-judging changes your behavior and causes the no — farmhouses hide whales, and forklift drivers hide foremen. Leads belong to the company, not to a salesman's opinion. C still ranks customers by guesswork.
principle_voice_en: When salespeople judge who will buy, their behavior changes and causes the customer not to buy.

scenario_en: A homeowner calls you directly — friend of a past customer: "I have three bids already. Just give me your number over the phone; if you're close, you're in." Your quote would be roughly 20% above the bids she read you. February is slow, the crews have gaps, and your new salesperson whispers, "Match the middle bid and lock it in."
option_a_en: Give her the rough number now with a phone discount — slow season, fill the crew.
option_b_en: Hold: no price before inspection and presentation. Earn the appointment, build the value, be proud of the number.
option_c_en: Decline politely — three bids in means she's a price shopper, not your customer.
why_en: A price with no value built is just a number to beat — once she has it, she doesn't need you. The HVLR company explains price once rather than apologizing for quality forever. Walking away pre-judges a referred lead.
principle_voice_en: We would rather explain price one time, than apologize for quality forever.

scenario_en: Your CRM audit finds 214 unsold proposals from the last 18 months — about $1.6M of work — untouched since each first "let me think about it." Your salespeople call follow-up "begging" and want fresh leads instead. Industry data on your wall says most of those homeowners bought, or will buy, from somebody within six months.
option_a_en: Run a one-week blitz on the freshest 50 and archive the rest.
option_b_en: Archive them — stale leads embarrass the brand; spend forward on new ones.
option_c_en: Build a forever follow-up system — Hunter role, schedule, scripts with new information, no file ever closed.
why_en: The most dangerous competitor never quits — every unsold proposal is paid-for gold being harvested by whoever calls. A blitz is an event; persistence is an identity, and identity is built into systems.
principle_voice_en: I will keep following up – forever, until the sale is made.

scenario_en: Career-best quarter: $380K profit on paper.
